item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Miguel Rojas Already Has New Job With Dodgers After Announcing Retirement
item.dc:creator: J P Hoornstra; Unknown
item.description: When Major League Baseball lost a Spanish-language World Series correspondent over the weekend, the Los Angeles Dodgers gained a player development staffer. item.content:encoded:
When Major League Baseball lost a Spanish-language World Series correspondent over the weekend, the Los Angeles Dodgers gained a player development staffer.
It's been a busy week for Miguel Rojas, who seems no less occupied with work now than he was a week ago — even if he's technically "retired."
The Dodgers' 2025 World Series hero shared an image to his Instagram story Monday from the team's Camelback Ranch facility.
Spring training is months away, but the Arizona Fall League is in full swing across the Phoenix basin. It's a logical place for Rojas to begin his post-playing career; Rojas already teased his plans to join the Dodgers' player development department long before he took his final at-bat.
Considering Rojas helped Mookie Betts with his transition from right field to shortstop only a couple years ago, it might not be a coincidence that he's in Glendale — where an erstwhile minor league outfielder, Charles Davalan, is embarking on a similar transition in the AFL.
Davalan, 22, was the Dodgers' first-round pick (41st overall) in the 2025 MLB Draft. He spent the entirety of his first two professional seasons as an outfielder, but is playing second base for the Glendale Desert Dogs.
Davalan has started 10 AFL games through Sunday, all at second base, and made three errors in 37 chances in the field.
For Rojas, the only surprise is the quick turnaround time between jobs. He played his final game for the Dodgers on Oct. 15, starting at second base in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series.
The Dodgers couldn't send that series back to Milwaukee, but Rojas went there anyway as a "special correspondent" with MLB's in-house media team at the World Series.
When the World Series shifted to St. Petersburg, Florida for Game 3 between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, Rojas headed to Arizona.
In addition to Davalan, seven other Dodgers prospects were assigned to play for the Glendale Desert Dogs in the AFL: third baseman Chase Harlan, catcher Anson Aroz and pitchers Marlon Nieves, Brooks Auger, Luke Fox, Sam Horn and Cody Morse.
Whatever Rojas can do to help the two infielders — Harlan and Davalan — could be time well-invested in the Dodgers' future defense.
In any case, it's remarkable to see any player transition from the field to the dugout so quickly.
Sign up for our free newsletter and follow us on X/Twitter and Facebook for the latest news.
J.P. Hoornstra is an On SI Contributor. A veteran of 20 years of sports coverage for daily newspapers in California, J.P. covered MLB, the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the Los Angeles Angels (occasionally of Anaheim) from 2012-23 for the Southern California News Group. His first book, The 50 Greatest Dodgers Games of All-Time, published in 2015. In 2016, he won an Associated Press Sports Editors award for breaking news coverage. He once recorded a keyboard solo on the same album as two of the original Doors.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have a secret club of veterans, revealed by Miguel Rojas, whose name stems from comments by the San Diego Padres team owner.
The secret Dodgers group
Rojas, appearing on MLB Network ahead of World Series Game 1, said he was close with four key veteran Dodgers: Mookie Betts, Max Muncy, Freddie Freeman, and Kike Hernandez.
All five are in their mid-to-late 30s and well into the second half of their careers. They have only a handful of seasons left at the top of baseball, and they were among the main examples of the Dodgers' roster housing "dinosaurs."
The Dodgers' roster age became a big topic of conversation after Padres owner Jose Feliciano, who bought the team a few months ago, said that "the owner of the Dodgers owns a lot of dinosaurs."
While Feliciano claimed to be talking about Dodgers owner Mark Walter's dinosaur fossil collection, the comment took on a life of its own, with Dodgers players all wearing dinosaur shirts.
Internally, Rojas and his core four teammates also named themselves after all the talk about the team's age.
"We're called the viejitos because they started calling us the dinosaurs, old players, old guys. They didn't know if we could still do it. In some form, we showed the world that we were able to do it," Rojas said.
How old were the Dodgers in 2026?
The Dodgers' average age, roster-wise, was 30.8, sitting highest in the league. The team's age came from the positional players.
The pitching side has plenty of youth, both organizationally and on the postseason roster.
The "Viejitos" do a fair amount to raise the average age, but other veterans throughout the lineup do little to add youth.
Heading into 2027, the roster's age remains a big talking point, and fans want the team to get younger.
With Rojas retiring, that already opens a slot for a younger player, while Kike Hernandez's future is still up in the air.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Miguel Rojas Reflects on Dodgers Career Immediately After Retirement

item.content:encoded:
Former Los Angeles Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas, who retired after the team fell in the NLCS this season, spoke about the impact his time with the Dodgers had on him.
Rojas is currently serving as a correspondent at the World Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, but also spared some time before the game to answer questions about himself.
“I told the players, the staff and the front office, not just thank you, they changed my life,” Rojas said. “They got me the opportunity to come back home to LA where I made my debut 12 years ago in 2014 and having the opportunity to live the best four years of my life in baseball.
“It wasn’t just for me, it was for my family, the people that I really care about. My son, they grabbed my son under their wing and they made growth with him. He was shagging balls in the outfield, he was living the dream. …That’s what I told the guys, thank you for changing my life.”
Rojas has sung the Dodgers’ praises the entire year, especially following his retirement. After his last game, the veteran expressed his desire to continue serving the team after stepping away from the sport.
“I want to stay here,” Rojas said. “I want to wear this uniform in a different capacity and continue to make the organization better.”
When Did Miguel Rojas Return to the Dodgers?
Rojas made his debut with the Dodgers in 2014, but the team traded him after his rookie year in a big deal with the Miami Marlins—during which the team also acquired Kiké Hernandez and Austin Barnes.
He stayed with the Marlins for nearly a decade, but the Dodgers decided to bring him back to the team in 2023, sending a minor-league infielder the other way.
Through his 446 games with the team from 2023-26, Rojas hit 22 homers and drove in 117 RBIs for the Dodgers, also posting a .688 OPS and hitting the biggest home run of his life. He stepped up to the plate in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series and hit a solo home run in the top of the ninth to tie the game and swing the momentum in the Dodgers’ favor as they went on to win their second consecutive World Series.
Rojas will forever be a Dodgers legend, and his constant praise of the organization shows how well the team treats their players.

item.description: Miguel Rojas isn’t done with baseball. item.content:encoded:
Miguel Rojas isn’t done with baseball.
The veteran infielder announced his retirement from Major League Baseball after the Dodgers were swept in the National League Championship Series by the Brewers. But Rojas will represent his home country one last time to play in the Venezuelan Professional Baseball League for the Tiburones de La Guaira club.
The Dodgers World Series hero will participate in special games for the team on Nov. 14 and 15 at LoanDepot Park in Miami.
Turns out Game 4 of the NLCS won’t be Rojas’ final game of his career.
“One last time on the field. One last time representing Venezuela,” Rojas said in an Instagram caption.
Rojas previously expressed disappointment with the World Baseball Classic after he was not able to participate in the spring tournament due to issues obtaining insurance on his MLB contract. The 37-year-old has never participated in a WBC and the 2026 tournament was his last chance before he retired.
“I didn’t know that my chance to go represent my country for the first and only time, probably as a player, was gonna get blocked because of an insurance problem,” Rojas said. “Even though we know we have to be ready for the season and we have to play and be healthy for our contract, at the end of the day, we didn’t know all those restrictions were gonna be in place the way they are right now.”
Rojas wasn’t able to represent Venezuela in the WBC, but he will play one last time for his home country next month.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Alex Vesia shares heartfelt message after difficult season
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Abdón Ibarra

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are entering a transitionary period this offseason, with a list of nine potential free agents that includes Alex Vesia among them.
Facing an uncertain future, the left-handed reliever took to Instagram to thank his teammates and fans for their support this season and over the past six years.
Vesia improved upon his 2025 season despite a regression in WHIP, walk rate and strikeout rate. He accomplished this thanks to a lower batting average against and cutting his home runs allowed by over half. That all came while attempting to move past personal tragedy for his family.
The 30-year-old was an important contributor to a Dodgers bullpen that finished in the top five in ERA.
He became one of L.A.’s most trusted relievers since joining the organization in 2021. Vesia has finished with a 2.64 ERA or lower in four of his six seasons with the Dodgers and posted a 2.87 ERA overall during that span.
A reunion makes sense for both sides, but is complicated by the future of the collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and the current state of the Dodgers’ roster.
The current CBA expires at 9 p.m. PT on Dec. 1. Players can sign new contracts prior to that point, but will be prohibited from doing so during an expected lockout that will likely drag well into 2027.
As for the Dodgers’ chances of re-signing Vesia, it could depend heavily on how his market develops. The organization is not likely to add another expensive bullpen contract with so much money invested in the group already.
An additional factor working against a reunion is how adept the front office is at identifying reliever talent. The Dodgers can allocate resources elsewhere if they can find a cheaper alternative.
Kiké Hernández’s posts potential goodbye to Dodgers fans
News of Miguel Rojas’ retirement leaves the Dodgers with eight decisions to make regarding potential free agents, one of which is Kiké Hernández.
Like Vesia, Hernández also took to social media to reflect on his time with the Dodgers.
The 35-year-old was open about his wish to re-sign with L.A. once again, but the chances of a deal materializing is not guaranteed.
The Dodgers’ other free agents this offseason include Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Tarik Skubal, and Blake Treinen.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Friedman Hopes Miguel Rojas Will Remain with Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Miguel Rojas may have played his final game in a Dodgers uniform, but Andrew Friedman hopes his association with the organization is far from over. During Wednesday’s season-ending press conference, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations praised the veteran infielder, who announced his retirement following the team’s elimination from the National League Championship Series against Milwaukee. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Miguel Rojas may have played his final game in a Dodgers uniform, but Andrew Friedman hopes his association with the organization is far from over.
During Wednesday’s season-ending press conference, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations praised the veteran infielder, who announced his retirement following the team’s elimination from the National League Championship Series against Milwaukee.
Rojas had expressed his desire to remain with the Dodgers in some capacity, and Friedman made it clear that the feeling is mutual.
“Miggy Ro has been awesome,” Friedman said. “Just his impact, not just on the field and the role he played.”
Rojas’s value to the Dodgers has extended well beyond his contributions at the plate or in the field. Over the past several seasons, he has become one of the organization’s most respected clubhouse leaders, serving as a mentor to both established veterans and young players trying to find their footing in the major leagues.
A Lasting Influence on Mookie Betts
Friedman specifically highlighted the role Rojas played in helping Mookie Betts make the difficult transition from right field to shortstop.
“Mookie’s ascension to the shortstop position, and not just being passable but being an above-average defender at short, Miggy Ro’s got his fingerprints around a lot of that,” Friedman explained.
It’s a significant compliment. Betts’s ability to reinvent himself defensively has been one of the more remarkable developments of his Dodgers career, and Rojas was instrumental in helping him learn the finer points of one of baseball’s most demanding positions.
Friedman also credited Rojas with mentoring young infielder Alex Freeland and helping establish the culture that has made the Dodgers so successful.
Those contributions aren’t necessarily reflected in the box scores, but they help explain why the organization values Rojas so highly.
A Career Comes Full Circle
Friedman also reflected on the unusual history he shares with Rojas.
“It’s funny because it was one of the first moves I did when I got here, was trading Miggy Ro away,” Friedman recalled.
Indeed, shortly after Friedman arrived in Los Angeles following the 2014 season, the Dodgers traded Rojas to the Miami Marlins as part of the deal that brought Kiké Hernández and other players to Los Angeles.
Eight years later, Rojas returned to the Dodgers, eventually becoming an important part of the teams that won back-to-back World Series championships in 2024 and 2025.
For Friedman, there was something particularly satisfying about seeing Rojas finish his playing career where it began.
“To kind of bookend his career and have him have a chance to come back and be such a big part of those two championship teams, and for him to go out the way he did, leaving everything on the field, can’t say enough about the guy, the competitor, the teammate,” Friedman said.
A New Role in Los Angeles?
Although Friedman didn’t announce any formal plans for Rojas, he expressed hope that the veteran would continue contributing to the organization.
“We’re hopeful that he’s impacting us in the future as well,” he said.
Given his experience, baseball knowledge and established relationships throughout the clubhouse, Rojas would seem like a natural candidate for a coaching, player development or advisory role.
His retirement closes an important chapter in Dodgers history, particularly for a team that has relied heavily on veteran leadership throughout its championship run.
But if Friedman gets his wish, Rojas will remain part of the Dodgers family.
And after everything he has contributed to the organization, that would be a fitting next chapter for one of the team’s most respected players.

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
Following Miguel Rojas’ retirement, the Los Angeles Dodgers eye a versatile trade target to bolster their depth.
Going out with a third straight World Series Championship would've been quite the story, but instead he announced his retirement after a heartbreaking Game 4 loss.
Here in 2026, Rojas played first, second, and third base, along with shortstop, and served as a designated hitter and pinch hitter for the Dodgers.
Dodgers could take a chance on McKinstry
This is the ultimate definition of buying low as McKinstry hit just .199 in '26.
For reference, the Ohio native played second and third base along with shortstop and all three outfield positions this past season.
McKinstry acted as both a pinch hitter and designated hitter as well, so he has incredible value defensively, even if he wasn't a tremendous hitter this year.
Miller called the Dodgers infield depth chart "pretty shallow," so going out and getting McKinstry would be an interesting option.
McKinstry has a ton of experience in the outfield, but this is a guy who spent a major chunk of the 2025 season at third base, and 2024 at shortstop.
In 2023, he split time evenly at second and third base along with right field, having 100+ at-bats at all three positions.
Below is a breakdown of his 2026 season with the number of at-bats he had at each position compared to Rojas's.
McKinstry's versatility in 2026
- Second base: 92 at-bats
- Third base: 16 at-bats
- Shortstop: 70 at-bats
- Left field: Four at-bats
- Center field: 14 at-bats
- Right field: 160 at-bats
Rojas's numbers in 2026
- First base: Three at-bats
- Second base: 107 at-bats
- Third base: 13 at-bats
- Shortstop: 63 at-bats
Seeing as McKinstry can play the outfield, and that's something Rojas hasn't done since 2014.
Trading for McKinstry doesn't feel like the big-splash move the Dodgers will need to return to the World Series, but bench players are extremely important, and this is definitely an option worth exploring.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers fell short of their ultimate goal in the postseason as the focus now shifts to a longer offseason than usual.
On the bright side, that means the front office doesn't have to rush as they decide which free agents to potentially bring back.
Among the team's eight free agents — after Miguel Rojas retired — is left-handed reliever Alex Vesia.
Vesia has been lights out since making his way to LA in 2021, and has a reputation of elevating his play in the postseason while bringing his infectious energy on the mound with emphatic battle cries and fist pumps after an inning-ending pitch.
Across the 2026 campaign, Vesia notched a 2.64 ERA over 72 appearances, the most in his seven-year career. He then allowed just one hit through five postseason outings.
Vesia turned 30 years old this past April and played last season on a $3.55 million club option the Dodgers happily exercised last November.
The hurler said via the Los Angeles Times' Maddie Lee that he would love to play (at least) a seventh season with LA.
“From the coaching staff, to the front office, to the players that have taken me under their wing, have helped mold and shape me into who I am and how I carry myself, how I go about my business,” Vesia said. “And if it wasn’t for the people in the room in this room, I would not be where I’m at today. So, very thankful. This whole experience has been life-changing.”
One of the hardest moments in Vesia's personal life held him out of last year's World Series. He and his wife Kayla announced the unfathomable loss of their first child, Sol. The support from the organization and its fans showed what a vital piece of the Dodgers community Vesia is.
He recently posted a message of gratitude to both fans and his teammates via his Instagram account detailing how difficult the past 12 months have been and how much the public outpour has meant in the year since his family's tragedy.
“By far the hardest year of my career. It's hard to put into words what this season was like. Personal battles with confidence, expectations and highs and lows mentally. I can't thank my teammates enough for picking me up on down days and dealing with my crazy ass on my high ones," he wrote. "I don't know what the future holds, but I do want to say thank you to Dodger Nation for showing me so much love over the past 6 years, especially this year. I'm just a man on a mission!”
How Much Will it Cost the Dodgers to Bring Alex Vesia Back?
Spotrac projects Vesia to earn a two-year, $14.2 million deal in free agency. It's possible he gets even more than that coming off multiple incredible seasons with LA.

item.content:encoded:
A LOS Angeles Dodgers star has sent a message to the fans after the World Series hero entered free agency.
The Dodgers were denied a chance at three consecutive World Series titles this year after they were brutally swept in the NLCS.
In a somewhat shocking affair, the Milwaukee Brewers got out the broom and brushed aside a $340 million payroll outfit inside three.
Just hours after the Brewers returned to the World Series for the first time since 1982, Dodgers hero Miguel Rojas announced his retirement.
And now it seems like more core members of the Dodgers’ back-to-back crew will be on their way out of LA.
The Dodgers have a number of stars hitting free agency, with star reliever Alex Vesia one of them.
READ MORE ON BASEBALL
After superstar pitcher Tarik Skubal, there is no player whose departure will hit harder than Vesia’s.
He has been an integral part of the Dodgers bullpen since 2021, but he has no idea whether he will be returning for the 2027 MLB season.
Vesia, 30, took to his Instagram to share a message with the Dodgers fanbase after their troubling defeat to the Brewers.
“By far the hardest year of my career. It’s hard to put into words what this season was like,” Vesia wrote in his Instagram caption.
How to watch the MLB post-season
MLB has new national TV deals for 2026-28 with ESPN, NBCUniversal, and Netflix. Several elements of MLB's national broadcast rights have not changed, including Fox, Warner Bros., and Apple Inc. deals for national coverage.
NBC returned to regular broadcast MLB coverage for the first time in 25 years. And Netflix made yet another significant move into live event coverage.
NBC: Sunday Night Baseball (moving from ESPN), Sunday Leadoff Games, whole Wild Card series, Labor Day primetime games and Opening Day primetime games
Netflix: Opening Night exclusive game, T-Mobile Home Run Derby, MLB at Field of Dreams Game (Beginning 2026), World Baseball Classic in Japan
ESPN: National midweek game package (30 games), secured the rights to sell and distribute MLB.TV into the ESPN app

“Personal battles with confidence, expectations and highs and lows mentally.
“I can’t thank my teammates enough for picking me up on down days and dealing with my crazy ass on my high ones.
“I don’t know what the future holds, but I do want to say thank you to Dodger Nation for showing me so much love over the past 6 years, especially this year. I’m just a man on a mission!”
Following his 2024 World Series heroics, allowing only one hit and one walk while striking out two in 2 and two-third scoreless innings, the next season was a tremendously tough one for Vesia.
He and his wife Kayla lost their newborn daughter right before the 2025 World Series in October that year, which he sat out of as a result.
Showing how much he meant to the team, Vesia’s teammates paid tribute by having his number 51 stitched into their caps for the World Series.
Despite his tough off-the-field situation, the 30-year-old bounced back with a 2.64 ERA across 72 appearances this season.
Vesia would certainly be missed by all of Dodgers nation should he be allowed to walk this offseason.

item.title: [abc7.com] Where 2026 ranks among best World Series matchups since 2000
item.dc:creator: David Schoenfield
item.description: This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played. The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS,
item.content:encoded:
This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played.
The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are in the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982 and seek the first championship in franchise history, looking to put an exclamation point on their season after leading the majors with 103 wins.
The Tampa Bay Rays were a 1998 expansion franchise and reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020 (the shortened season during the COVID-19 pandemic) but are seeking their first title as well. Young power hitter Junior Caminero and unheralded staff ace Drew Rasmussen lead the way as the Rays look to finally cash in after making the playoffs six times in the past eight seasons.
The Brewers and Rays led their respective leagues in wins, always a bonus for those who want the best teams in the World Series. Of course, a lot of attention will be given to the small-market aspect of the matchup, as the cloud of the lockout looms in the offseason.
Let's rank all the World Series since 2000 to see where Brewers-Rays fits in. This ranking is based on hype, the quality of the teams and their star power heading into the World Series. It's not a ranking of the quality of the World Series itself, although we're going to include a grade on that for each matchup. Let's get to it.
The Yankees were back in the World Series for the sixth time in eight years, and the Marlins had rebuilt after their fire sale following their World Series title in 1997. Trust me when I say that nobody wanted the Yankees in the World Series yet again. And the Marlins were merely a 91-win wild-card team. Most notably, however, both teams had spoiled the ultimate World Series by knocking off the Cubs and Red Sox -- before either team had overcome its curse -- in Game 7s in the LCS.
Actual World Series: C. The Marlins won Game 4 in 12 innings, when Yankees manager Joe Torre inexplicably failed to use reliever Mariano Rivera, and then 23-year-old Josh Beckett tossed a five-hit shutout in Game 6.
In an all-wild-card series, the fifth-seeded Rangers had won 90 games and the sixth-seeded Diamondbacks won only 84, making this the lowest combined win total in World Series history (for full seasons). The Rangers were going for their first World Series title, so there was that, and there were some fun hitters -- Corey Seager, the red-hot Adolis Garcia (who had just driven in 15 runs in the ALCS) and Corbin Carroll -- but it was a soft matchup on paper.
Actual World Series: D-. The series turned on Seager's tying two-run homer off Paul Sewald in the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, which Garcia then won with a home run in the 11th. There wasn't a single lead change after that, and three of those games were blowouts.
This was the Cardinals team that got hot in September and clinched a wild-card spot on the final day of the season when the Braves blew a lead in the ninth inning and lost in extra innings. St. Louis certainly had star power with the likes of Albert Pujols, Lance Berkman and Matt Holliday but had won a World Series fairly recently (2006), and the Rangers had just been there the year before.
Actual World Series: A. The first two games were one-run games, including the Rangers pulling out a victory with two runs in the ninth. In Game 3, Pujols blasted a record-tying three home runs. Game 6 was the David Freese Game -- perhaps the single most exciting baseball game ever played. Game 7 was a bit of an anticlimactic 6-2 Cardinals win.
The second-lowest combined win total in World Series history featured two wild-card teams that won fewer than 90 games. The Royals were at least a good story -- in the playoffs for the first time since winning the World Series in 1985 -- and had gone 8-0 in the AL playoffs, including an epic win over the A's in the wild-card game. The Giants, however, had just won the World Series in 2010 and 2012, and this team didn't seem nearly as good as those two.
Actual World Series: B-. Five of the games were blowouts, but it did at least go seven. It'll be remembered for Madison Bumgarner's historic performance: a shutout in Game 5 (the last complete game shutout in World Series history) and then five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, getting Salvador Perez to pop out with the tying run on third to end it.
The Red Sox were only three years removed from breaking the Curse of the Bambino in 2004, so although they were still a star-laden team with David Ortiz, Manny Ramirez and scrappy rookie Dustin Pedroia, they were no longer as interesting. The Rockies were a fun story, winning 14 of their final 15 games, including beating the Padres in a tiebreaker, just to win a wild-card spot. Then they went 7-0 in the NL playoffs and had won 21 of 22 entering the World Series.
Actual World Series: F.A dud. Two of the games were one-run games, but this goes down as one of the least memorable World Series of all time, with a forgettable four-game sweep.
The Tigers were the story of the season. They had lost 119 games three years before and 91 just the previous year. With rookie starter Justin Verlander winning 17 games, they led the AL Central most of the season -- only to lose their final five games and squeak into the playoffs as a wild-card team. The Cardinals won a weak NL Central with only 83 wins -- although they at least had Pujols at his absolute peak (.331/.431/.671, 49 home runs). Both teams hadn't won a World Series in a couple of decades: 1982 for the Cardinals, 1984 for the Tigers. Plus, it did feature two of the original 16 franchises.
Actual World Series: F. The Cardinals won one game in the bottom of the eighth, but it was otherwise a blur of nothing, most characterized by several fielding miscues by Tigers pitchers. David Eckstein won MVP honors without hitting a home run and while driving in only four runs.
The Braves were back in the World Series for the first time since 1999 -- they had made 12 playoff appearances in the intervening years without making it to the Fall Classic. Still, this was the weakest of the Atlanta playoff teams of recent vintage, winning only 88 games and missing Ronald Acuña Jr. for the playoffs. The Astros, meanwhile, were back in the World Series for the third time in five years -- but the first time since the 2017 sign-stealing scandal had broken in November 2019. Let's just say not everyone wanted them there.
Actual World Series: D. This was a weird World Series. The Braves ended up going with two bullpen games (who remembers that Dylan Lee and Tucker Davidson started?) after Charlie Morton broke a leg in Game 1. Astros starters kept getting knocked out early (the only starter to go more than five innings for either team was Max Fried in the finale). Four of the games were blowouts.
The Giants were back after winning in 2010, and the Tigers were back for the first time since 2006, featuring Triple Crown winner Miguel Cabrera and a strong 1-2 punch in the rotation with Verlander and Max Scherzer. This was also the last World Series with that season's MVP winners until Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani in 2024, with Cabrera and Buster Posey.
Actual World Series: D-. A boring sweep. Pablo Sandoval did hit three home runs in Game 1, but there were two shutouts and chilly weather in Detroit made the final two games unbearable.
This one did feature the two best teams from the regular season (both won 97 games), the last time before this year that we had that happen in a full season. It was also a classic original-16 matchup, although we had seen this in 2004 -- plus, both teams had won recently (2007 for Boston, 2011 for St. Louis). These were veteran teams, with Ortiz leading the Red Sox and the Cardinals featuring four .300 hitters, plus Carlos Beltran, who hit .296 and led the team in home runs.
Actual World Series: C+. Ortiz was absolutely locked in, hitting .688/.760/1.188 with two home runs and eight walks. The Cardinals were so scared of him by Game 6 that they intentionally walked him three times -- with two of those helping lead to rallies and a 6-1 Red Sox victory in the final game.
This one could be No. 25 -- it was during the pandemic, after all, and it was played at a neutral site in a half-empty stadium for social distancing reasons. But it was a great matchup between the teams with the best records in each league, albeit over the shortened 60-game season. You had Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw and Randy Arozarena in the midst of one of the best postseasons ever, plus the small-market Rays trying to beat the big-market Dodgers.
Actual World Series: C+. Because teams were allowed an expanded roster of 28 players, it was a parade of relievers -- but there were some fun games, including a bonkers ending to Game 4 and then Rays manager Kevin Cash's controversial decision to remove Blake Snell in Game 6, which backfired in a big way.
Maybe this should rate higher. After all, at the time, the White Sox were trying to break a World Series drought going back to 1917 and the Astros, born in 1962, had never won. But the White Sox's drought never had the same nationwide interest as the ones for the Cubs or Red Sox (fair or not) and these weren't particularly interesting teams. The White Sox were very good -- they won 99 games -- but lacked star power, with Paul Konerko their biggest name (Frank Thomas was on the team that year but played only 34 games and was injured for the playoffs). The Astros had Yankees transplants Roger Clemens and Andy Pettitte, but their two longtime stars, Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, were at the end of their careers (Bagwell, in his final season, was relegated to DH and pinch-hitting duties).
Actual World Series: C. It's hard to give a sweep a decent grade, but all four games were exciting, including Scott Podsednik's walk-off home run in Game 2 (after not hitting a home run all season) and Geoff Blum's go-ahead home run in the 14th inning to win Game 3.
The Phillies were back in the World Series for the first time since 1993 -- and hadn't won since 1980. They featured a powerful offense with Chase Utley, Ryan Howard, Jimmy Rollins and Pat Burrell. The Rays were maybe the unlikeliest World Series team ever: In their 10 previous years of existence, they had not only never had a winning season but had lost at least 90 games in each one. They won 97 games that year behind rookie Evan Longoria and power-hitting first baseman Carlos Peña, with speedsters Carl Crawford and B.J. Upton in the outfield.
Actual World Series: D+. Three games were decided by one run, but it was a pretty uneventful World Series. The lasting memory is the cold and rain in Philly that forced the midgame postponement of Game 5, the only time that has happened in World Series history. The game was suspended in the sixth inning and resumed two days later.
A Subway Series -- the first since the Yankees and Brooklyn Dodgers met in 1956 -- was certainly fun for the Big Apple, but it was less fun for the rest of the country (it drew the worst TV ratings at the time). The Yankees were going for a third straight World Series and had officially become the Evil Empire by that point. To make it even worse, they weren't even that good that season, winning only 87 games. The Mets were back in the World Series for the first time since 1986. There was certainly plenty of star power all around with the likes of Derek Jeter, Roger Clemens and Mike Piazza.
Actual World Series: C+. It was a tight-fought five-game series with all games decided by two runs or fewer. The turning point was the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, when the Yankees tied it off Armando Benitez and went on to win in 12 innings. Game 2 featured the infamous Clemens-Piazza bat-throwing incident, and the Yankees won the clincher with two runs in the ninth off a tired Al Leiter.
I know, the Astros ... again. Boo. But this was an absolute powerhouse of a team with 106 wins and stars such asYordan Alvarez (1.019 OPS) and Verlander (18-4, 1.75 ERA), plus the old standbys Jose Altuve and Alex Bregman. The Phillies, meanwhile, snuck in as a wild-card team for their first playoff trip since 2011 but were an immensely entertaining team with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber& Co., as well as a passionate fanbase cheering them on.
Actual World Series: C. The Phillies won 6-5 in Game 1 on J.T. Realmuto's home run in the 10th inning. They took a 2-1 series lead, but then their bats died. Astros pitchers tossed a combined no-hitter to even the series, and Houston won the final two games 3-2 and 4-1, with Alvarez's three-run blast in Game 6 the deciding blow.
The Brewers' drought is the big narrative here as they try to finally cash in after their past decade of success, but we're still getting the 103-win Brewers facing the 98-win Rays, the best combined win total in the World Series since the Astros and Dodgers in 2017. (Not to mention we get a first-time winner no matter the outcome.) The Brewers aren't your conventional powerhouse team -- relying on speed, defense, timely hitting and a dominant bullpen -- but they do have one of the biggest stars of the 2026 season in Jacob Misiorowski, plus a rising star in young Jackson Chourio. The Rays might lack big names, although Junior Caminero is just the second player with two 40-homer seasons by age 22, and like the Brewers, they're trying to finally win it all after years of success.
Actual World Series: To be determined.
The Royals proved their 2014 World Series appearance was no fluke, winning 95 games with a better team that included trade deadline additions Ben Zobrist and Johnny Cueto. The Mets won the NL East behind a young, powerful rotation that featured Matt Harvey, Noah Syndergaard and Jacob deGrom. It was a fun matchup of teams trying to avoid lengthy title droughts -- 30 years for the Royals, 29 for the Mets.
Actual World Series: C+. It went only five games, but the Royals won the opener in 14 innings, won Game 5 with a three-run eighth inning and then won the clincher in 12 innings -- after Mets manager Terry Collins' ill-fated decision to leave in Harvey to start the ninth with a 2-0 lead.
This was a super entertaining showdown at the time. The Giants had yet to win a World Series in San Francisco and featured Tim Lincecum ("The Freak," for his small stature and overpowering stuff) and two rookies named Posey and Bumgarner. The Rangers had never won a championship and featured AL MVP Josh Hamilton and veteran DH Vladimir Guerrero. Both teams had pulled off upsets in the LCS, with the Giants beating the Phillies and the Rangers beating the Yankees.
Actual World Series: D. Meh. The Giants won the opener in a blowout as the Rangers made four errors and then tossed shutouts in Games 2 (behind Matt Cain) and 4 (behind Bumgarner). You can test Giants fans by asking them who won World Series MVP honors that year. Answer: Edgar Renteria (he hit .412 with two home runs and six RBIs).
Remember, this happened before the sign-stealing scandal changed how we view this era of the Astros. They had won 107 games behind the pitching duo of Verlander and Gerrit Cole and four players who mashed 30-plus home runs (which didn't even include Alvarez, a rookie that year). The Nationals were a wild-card team that had overcome a 19-31 season start to win 93 games and featured a starting pitching trio of Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin (and 20-year-old sensation Juan Soto, who hit 34 home runs).
Actual World Series: B-. It went seven games -- the road team would win all seven -- although five of the games weren't close. The best game was the last one: The Nationals went ahead 3-2 in the seventh inning on Anthony Rendon's home run and then Howie Kendrick's go-ahead home run just inside the right-field foul pole.
This matchup began with a lot of hype: Shohei Ohtani, coming off his all-time game in the NLCS in which he hit three home runs and struck out 10 batters as the starting pitcher, against Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who had hit .442 with six home runs through the first two rounds of the playoffs. The Dodgers were looking to become the first team with back-to-back titles since the 2000 Yankees and the first NL team since the 1976 Reds. The Blue Jays were back in the World Series for the first time since Joe Carter walked off the Phillies in 1993. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts stirred things up after the NLCS when he said during the postgame celebration, "Let's get four more wins and really ruin baseball" -- a reference to the criticism of the Dodgers' high payroll.
Actual World Series: A+. The Dodgers won Game 3 in 18 innings on Freddie Freeman's walk-off home run, which followed an unlikely four-inning relief performance from Will Klein, the last guy on the Dodgers' staff. The Dodgers went back to Toronto trailing 3-2 but won Game 6 behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto and a crazy game-ending double play.
Game 7 featured two future Hall of Famers starting in Ohtani and Max Scherzer, more on-the-edge-of-your-seat plays than any game in World Series history, Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run in the ninth to tie it, as well as Will Smith's go-ahead one in the 11th -- and finally, Yamamoto pitching in relief to close out the game by inducing a double play with two runners on to win it for the Dodgers. It wasn't quite the greatest World Series overall, but two all-time games made it a classic.
The Angels, who joined the majors in 1961, were making their first World Series appearance, while the Giants, in the Bay Area since 1958, were trying to win their first title since moving from New York. You had Barry Bonds at the height of his unstoppable powers -- and trying to erase his own postseason demons -- while the Angels had a loaded lineup (Troy Glaus, Tim Salmon, Garret Anderson), the Rally Monkey and those deafening ThunderStix (let us pray they never return).
Actual World Series: A. Bonds was a beast, hitting .471/.700/1.294 (yes, that's a 1.994 OPS), but it wasn't enough. This series featured four one-run games, including a wild 11-10 contest and the classic Game 6, when the Angels rallied late from a 5-0 deficit to win 6-5. Game 7 was a drab 4-1 contest (Bonds went a harmless 1-for-3).
The Yankees had missed the playoffs in 2008 for the first time since 1993, so they went out and signed free agents CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett to add to an already stacked roster that included Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Robinson Cano, Hideki Matsui, Jorge Posada and Johnny Damon. Whoa. Yes, they were still the Evil Empire. The Phillies, trying to defend their title, had traded for Cliff Lee and then signed Pedro Martinez in July to bolster their rotation.
Actual World Series: C. It could have been a classic battle, but there were no one-run games and Game 6 -- Martinez's final start of his career -- was over early. The crucial contest was Game 4, when the Yankees scored three runs in the ninth off Phillies closer Brad Lidge to win 7-4.
This one presented conflicting emotions. The Yankees were going for an unthinkable fourth straight title, but in the wake of 9/11, there was a "Win it for New York" angle that the Yankees had never encountered. The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, had the big, bad duo of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling. When asked on the eve of the World Series about the Yankees' mystique and aura, Schilling provided one of the great quips in World Series history: "Mystique and Aura? Those are dancers at a nightclub." The Diamondbacks were not going to be intimidated.
Actual World Series: A+. Four one-run games, including three of the most memorable World Series moments ever: Jeter's Mr. November home run to win Game 4, Scott Brosius' walk-off home run to win Game 5 and then Luis Gonzalez's bloop single to beat the invincible Mariano Rivera in Game 7.
Two of baseball's most historic franchises had never met in a World Series, creating the classic showdown with games in Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium. It doesn't get any better than that. The Red Sox were a 108-win powerhouse -- with AL MVP Mookie Betts leading the way, backed up by J.D. Martinez, who hit .330 with 43 home runs that season. Chris Sale and David Price headlined the rotation. The Dodgers actually had a bit of a down year with 92 wins, but they also weren't lacking in big names, with Manny Machado (a trade deadline acquisition), Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Cody Bellinger and Justin Turner, with Kershaw and rookie Walker Buehler on the pitching side.
Actual World Series: C-. A letdown. The first two games in Fenway were cold and windy. Game 3 was an 18-inning affair -- the longest in World Series history -- but was more of a slog than a game to remember. Game 4 was the best of the series as the Red Sox rallied with nine runs over the final three innings to win 9-6.
This series had it all: dominant teams (both won over 100 games), long World Series title droughts (never for the Astros, 1988 for the Dodgers) and superstars galore (Altuve, Verlander, Carlos Correa, Kershaw, Seager, Bellinger, Yu Darvish). We didn't know at the time that both franchises were just kicking off 100-win dynasties -- let alone what the Astros were doing behind the scenes -- but the anticipation level was off the charts for the first matchup of 100-win teams in the World Series since 1970.
Actual World Series: A-. Game 1, with a start-time temperature of 103 degrees at Dodger Stadium, was a Kershaw 11-strikeout gem. The Astros tied Game 2 in the ninth on Marwin Gonzalez's home run off Kenley Jansen (1.32 ERA that season), both teams scored twice in the 10th, the Astros scored twice in the 11th on George Springer's home run and held on for a 7-6 win. Game 4 featured a five-run rally in the ninth by the Dodgers to win. Game 5 was completely bananas, with the Astros finally winning 13-12 in 10 innings. Game 7 was a letdown though, as the Astros won a 5-1 snoozer in which they scored five runs off Darvish in the first two innings.
As mentioned, what's not to like? Aside from Ohtani and Judge each playing in their first World Series and trying to put a final stamp on their legacy-defining seasons, we hadJuan Soto and Mookie Betts, a suddenly rejuvenated Giancarlo Stanton and a hobbled Freddie Freeman (only raising the drama if he hit well), Gerrit Cole and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Aside from the history between the clubs, we had both clubs needing to rewrite their recent history: The Yankees, back in the World Series for the first time since 2009, and the Dodgers trying to add a more legitimate championship to the one they won in the COVID-shortened season.
Actual World Series:C+. The Judge-Ohtani showdown was a flop, as Judge hit .222 with one home run and Ohtani hit .105 without a home run or RBI. The series also went just five games, with the Dodgers winning the first three. The series did produce two forever moments, however: Freeman's walk-off, Kirk Gibson-esque grand slam in Game 1 and the Yankees' fifth-inning defensive meltdown in Game 5.
The Red Sox were coming off their never-done-before comeback from down 3-0 to beat the Yankees in the ALCS -- and still had to beat a 105-win Cardinals team that featured Pujols (.331, 46 home runs), Jim Edmonds (.301, 42 home runs) and Scott Rolen (.314, 34 home runs), plus in-season pickup Larry Walker, who had an OPS over 1.000 that year. The Red Sox had their own ridiculous lineup with Ortiz (.301, 41 home runs), Ramirez (.308, 43 home runs) and Damon (.304, 20 home runs) plus a rotation with Schilling and Martinez. It seems inevitable now that Boston was going to win, but that wasn't the case at the time, so the buildup was intense.
Actual World Series: D. Blah. I mean, Red Sox fans will rightfully call it the best World Series ever, but after a sloppy 11-9 Game 1 played in a drizzle at Fenway (the Red Sox won despite committing four errors), the Cardinals never led again.
The Cubs had not only not won since 1908, but they hadn't even been in a World Series since 1945. The Guardians, meanwhile, had the second-longest drought of the original 16 teams, without a title since 1948. That was enough right there to build up the anticipation, but this also rates high because it was two good teams -- Chicago won 104 games while Cleveland won 94. Cubs third baseman Kris Bryant won MVP honors that year and Cleveland was led by 18-game winner Corey Kluber (who would start three times) and young rising stars Francisco Lindor and Jose Ramirez.
Actual World Series: B. The first six games weren't anything too special, but Game 7 was one of the greatest in World Series history. Cleveland tied it on Rajai Davis' three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth, the Cubs scored twice in the 10th -- following a stress-filled rain delay -- and escaped with an 8-7, curse-ending win when Cleveland had to bat little-used Michael Martinez with its season on the line.
]

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Skubal & Kiké Headlight Dodgers 2027 Free Agent Class
item.dc:creator: Cody Snavely

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—While the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason remains in play, the offseason has officially begun for the Los Angeles Dodgers after their anticlimactic series sweep at the hands of the National League champion Milwaukee Brewers.
After the conclusion of the 2026 Fall Classic, the Dodgers are set to have a total of nine free agents hit the open market, an increase from five last season.
While the list reads as nine, it is essentially eight, as veteran infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball after the Dodgers’ Game Four loss.
Free Agents
(9): Blake Treinen, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Alex Vesia, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Tarik Skubal
Blake Treinen
Veteran right-hander Blake Treinen’s season ended during the final week of September after a right shoulder setback that forced him off the Dodgers postseason roster.
Treinen returned to Los Angeles after his 2024 World Series heroics on a 2-year, $14 million contract, and now the 38-year-old will be without a home entering an offseason that may be the final season of his career.
Evan Phillips
Right-hander Evan Phillips missed all of 2025 and returned toward the middle of the 2026 regular season due to Tommy John surgery. However, in his games played, he was very effective, going 3-2 with a 3.46 ERA.
Still, Phillips will be entering his age 33 season and has already missed significant time due to right elbow/arm injuries, and with multiple pitchers in the pipeline, it’s not hard to see the Dodgers moving on.
Kris Bubic
Acquired at the trade deadline, left-hander Kris Bubic is likely to get a contract this Winter as a starter, since that was his primary role before injuries derailed his 2026 season.
Bubic was an All-Star in 2025 and, with a thin free-agent market, could land a nice contract from a team desperate for starting pitching.
Miguel Rojas
Shortly after the conclusion of Game Four of the NLCS, veteran utility infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball, bringing an end to his 13-year playing career.
Rojas is expected to remain with the Dodgers organization in a player devleopment/coaching role.
Kiké Hernández
October hero Kiké Hernández is hitting free agency yet again this Winter, and after a subpar performance in October, minus one huge home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS, not much is known about whether the Dodgers will try to run it back for another 1-year deal.
Overall, Hernández missed most of the season while recovering from elbow surgery and an oblique injury and hit 4 home runs in 90 at-bats while posting a below-average 82 OPS+.
The fan favorite will enter his age-36 season, likely ending his Dodgers tenure for the second time.
Alex Vesia
Arguably the biggest free agent from the Dodgers bullpen this Winter is left-hander Alex Vesia, who has likely pitched his way to a sizable multi-year contract that the Dodgers might not be inclined to match.
Vesia, 30, posted an elite 2.64 ERA and struck out 74 batters despite a below-average fastball velocity, but with backend pitching at a premium, his market is likely to be heavy.
Brusdar Graterol
Brusdar Graterol’s career has been defined by injuries, and that likely will force his time in Dodger Blue to come to an end this Winter.
Despite a 2.78 career ERA, the right-hander has pitched only 7.1 innings for the Dodgers since the 2024 regular season, missing the entire 2025 and 2026 seasons due to right shoulder surgery.
Eric Lauer
Like Bubic, left-hander Eric Lauer will enter the market as a starting pitcher, and after a second-half renaissance with the Dodgers, where he went 7-2 with a 4.50 ERA, he could be a dependable backend starter to eat innings for a variety of clubs.
Tarik Skubal
The consensus No. 1 free agent this Winter across baseball is two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is set to demand a massive multi-year contract that could go north of $400 million.
While the Dodgers will no doubt be involved, it’s hard to imagine them matching that while already having so many long-term deals tied up, especially in their starting rotation already.
Skubal is likely to sign before the MLB lockout on December 1st to maximize his contract, such as fellow Scott Boras client Corey Seager did after the 2021 season.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
Cody Snavely has been the co-editor of DodgersBeat and full-time host of the Bleed Los Podcast since February 2023. He has also written for multiple websites, such as Dodgers Way, Dodgers Low-Down, and Dodgers Tailgate. A Wilmington University graduate, Snavely is an avid Dodgers fan who uses his advanced baseball knowledge to keep fans updated on the latest storylines, rumors, and opinions on Dodgers baseball.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Hyeseong Kim apologizes to Dodgers fans for disappointing season
item.dc:creator: Blake Williams

item.content:encoded:
During Spring Training, Hyeseong Kim was in the running to be the Los Angeles Dodgers’ starting second baseman while Tommy Edman was out. Instead, the job went to Alex Freeland.
Kim opened the year in Triple-A and didn’t spend much time with the Dodgers. He appeared in just 43 games and didn’t produce much when given the opportunity.
Kim hit just .259/.323/.328 with one home run, 16 runs scored, 11 RBI, five stolen bases and an 83 wRC+. In the Minors, he wasn’t much better either, slashing .262/.330/.345 with a 77 wRC+ in the hitter-friendly Pacific Coast League.
After a poor season, Kim shared a message on Instagram apologizing for his struggles on the field, thanking fans and the Dodgers for their support, and committing to be better in 2027.
Hello, this is Hyeseong Kim!
Looking back on this season, I’m sorry I couldn’t show you better performances, and I was deeply disappointed in myself as well. Still, I sincerely thank everyone who supported me through it all.
I love the Dodgers, and I have never once been disappointed in this team. It was my choice, and I haven’t regretted it for a single moment. My only disappointment was in myself. I have nothing but gratitude for the team and all the Dodgers fans!
Next year, I will strive to become a better person and a better baseball player. Thank you!😊👍
Kim enters an important year for both his future with the Dodgers and potentially his MLB career. The 2027 season is the final year of his three-year, $12.5 million contract before the Dodgers have club options in 2028 and 2029.
The Dodgers would certainly move on with another poor season from Kim, and there’s no guarantee he even makes it through the offseason in the organization.
If he hits like he did in 2026, other organizations may also just view him as just Minor League depth, putting a lot of pressure on him heading into the new season.
However, the Dodgers have open spots on their bench with Miguel Rojas retiring and Kiké Hernández reaching free agency with the club likely to move on. The additional roster spots could bode well for Kim’s chances of sticking around.
The Dodgers also need to get younger, and Kim will be just 28 years old entering the 2027 season. In addition, he provides a speed element to the roster that no one else does.
Kim’s ability to play the middle infield could also help his chances of sticking around with the Dodgers losing two infielders who served bench roles, but he would also compete with Freeland once again for that role.
But even with his speed and defensive ability, Kim still needs to hit to be on a Major League roster, and his production from 2026 won’t cut it.
In 2025, Kim was still a below-league-average hitter, but he had the benefit of the doubt after moving from South Korea to the United States and facing tougher competition. Now, Kim doesn’t have any excuses, and it’ll be up to him to prove himself as a Major Leaguer.
Dodgers working with Hyeseong Kim’s swing mechanics
Since signing Kim, the Dodgers have been working on his swing mechanics to develop more consistency and pop. That has been ongoing for two seasons now, and they believed his mechanics were the cause of some of his 2026 struggles.
An offseason of working on his swing and resetting could prove beneficial, but with the impending lockout, Kim will not be able to work with Dodgers hitting coaches once it begins, adding another obstacle.
If you love our reporting, choose DodgerBlue.com as a preferred source on Google.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ÁNGELES - La temporada baja ha llegado antes de lo previsto para los Dodgers.
Antes de haber asimilado por completo la derrota del jueves por la noche (6-4) ante los Cerveceros en el Juego 4 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional —resultado que puso fin a su temporada y a su intento de lograr un tercer título consecutivo—, los Dodgers tuvieron que afrontar la realidad de que probablemente se avecinan cambios en el equipo.
Los Dodgers perderán a nueve jugadores debido a la agencia libre, un grupo encabezado por la figura más destacada del mercado, Tarik Skubal. Los otros jugadores que pronto serán agentes libres son el venezolano Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen, Eric Lauer, Kris Bubic y el venezolano Brusdar Graterol.
Gran parte del núcleo del equipo de Los Ángeles permanecerá intacto en el futuro previsible, por lo que la ventana competitiva no se está cerrando; sin embargo, este podría ser un periodo de transición entre una era del béisbol de los Dodgers y otra.
"Nunca puedes pensar que este es el final", dijo Rojas, quien permanecerá en la organización desempeñando un papel en el desarrollo de jugadores. "Y conozco muy bien a esta organización; no se conformarán con esta derrota".
A lo largo de 14 participaciones consecutivas en la postemporada, los Dodgers han encontrado formas fluidas de incorporar talento joven a sus plantillas para complementar a su núcleo de veteranos experimentados. Ese proceso ya ha comenzado con el dominicano Josue De Paula —el prospecto número 4 a nivel general según MLB Pipeline—, así como con el receptor suplente Dalton Rushing y el jugador de cuadro Alex Freeland.
No obstante, es posible que los Dodgers deban adoptar un enfoque más deliberado para asignar roles más destacados a sus jugadores jóvenes de cara al futuro, lo que dará lugar a decisiones interesantes durante esta temporada baja.
"No conocemos el futuro", comentó el dominicano Teóscar Hernández. "Pero algo que sabemos es que nos preocupamos los unos por los otros, nos cuidamos mutuamente y nos apoyamos durante todo el año... Este grupo es realmente especial, no por lo que hemos logrado en los últimos dos años y en este, sino simplemente por la unión que tenemos".
A continuación, un vistazo a algunas de las decisiones más importantes sobre el roster que deberán tomar los Dodgers durante esta temporada baja:
¿Participarán en la puja por Skubal?
Los Dodgers se desprendieron de dos prospectos clasificados entre los 100 mejores —el abridor listo para las Grandes Ligas River Ryan y el jardinero Zyhir Hope—, además del lanzador derecho Brady Smith, a cambio de contar con Skubal por un periodo de hasta tres meses. No fueron el único equipo dispuesto a hacer una gran inversión por un talento del calibre de Skubal, y lo mismo ocurrirá cuando este llegue al mercado de agentes libres por primera vez.
Skubal ganó su caso de arbitraje salarial contra los Tigres la temporada baja pasada, obteniendo un salario récord de US$32 millones. Se espera ampliamente que consiga la mayor cantidad de dinero garantizado jamás otorgada a un lanzador en la agencia libre, superando el contrato de 12 años y US$325 millones de Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
En su año previo a la agencia libre, Skubal se perdió seis semanas tras someterse a una cirugía en el codo izquierdo, pero aun así completó otra campaña sólida, registrando una marca de 12-7 y una efectividad de 2.72 en 26 aperturas con los Tigres y los Dodgers. Prefirió no hablar sobre su futuro inmediatamente después de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional (SCLN).
"Sí, realmente no voy a hacer comentarios sobre mi futuro", dijo Skubal. "El día de hoy es una porquería, ya sabes, y en eso es en lo que estoy pensando ahora mismo".
Aun así, Skubal expresó su agradecimiento por el tiempo que pasó con los Dodgers.
"Una organización increíble, compañeros increíbles, una afición increíble", dijo. "Es un honor llevar las letras 'L.A.' en el pecho y en la gorra".
¿Cómo le darán tiempo de juego para De Paula?
En septiembre, De Paula hizo que el salto de Doble-A a las Grandes Ligas pareciera sencillo, impresionando tanto a los Dodgers que logró entrar en el roster de postemporada como opción de bateador emergente. Sin embargo, su limitación radicaba en que el equipo de Grandes Ligas lo veía únicamente como bateador designado, una posición ocupada por Shohei Ohtani.
"Creo que la mejora que Josue mostró en los jardines entre 2025 y 2026 es real", comentó el mes pasado Andrew Friedman, presidente de operaciones de béisbol. "Y para nosotros, se trata de dar otro gran paso de cara a 2027. Él tiene las herramientas y la capacidad para lograrlo".
Con el tiempo, los Dodgers tendrán que poner a De Paula a jugar en los jardines. No obstante, sus jardineros titulares —Teóscar Hernández, el cubano Andy Pages y Kyle Tucker— tienen contrato vigente hasta la próxima temporada.
Si los Dodgers consideran que De Paula está listo para ser jugador titular habitual, eso probablemente implicaría, como mínimo, limitar el tiempo de juego de Hernández. También podría darse una medida más drástica: buscar un equipo interesado en asumir la última temporada garantizada de su contrato de tres años y US$66 millones.
Otra opción sería que De Paula comenzara la temporada en Triple-A, donde podría trabajar en su defensa en un entorno de menor presión.
¿Qué jugadores veteranos clave regresarán?
Entre los agentes libres inminentes, algunas de las bajas más significativas en cuanto a liderazgo serían Kiké Hernández, Phillips, Vesia y Treinen. El bullpen ciertamente podría tener hueco para lanzadores de situaciones críticas como Phillips y Vesia, pero el encaje de Hernández entre los jugadores de posición no está tan claro.
Hernández, el propio "Mr. October" de los Dodgers, tuvo una temporada regular marcada por las lesiones. Tampoco estuvo a la altura de su habitual rendimiento en postemporada, conectando apenas un jonrón solitario en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional (SDLN) como único imparable. Es una figura importante en el vestuario y, aunque le encantaría volver a Los Ángeles, sabe que sus necesidades y las del equipo deben coincidir durante la agencia libre.
"Me encantaría intentarlo una vez más, tratar de ganar otro", dijo Hernández. "Pero realmente no sé qué va a pasar. Espero volver y, si no es así, espero poder jugar en un equipo ganador".

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers 2026 report card: Shohei Ohtani gets an F, only two hitters receive an A
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: The Dodgers won 100 games this season. They claimed the National League West division yet again. But, after reaching the National League Championship Series, their World Series three-peat bid flamed out in a sweep to the Brewers. In the wake of their elimination, The California Post graded the season of every player on the Dodgers’ roster. First up, the offense, which ranked top-five in the regular season in scoring, batting average and OPS –– but faltered in the playoffs and was shut down in th
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers won 100 games this season. They claimed the National League West division yet again. But, after reaching the National League Championship Series, their World Series three-peat bid flamed out in a sweep to the Brewers.
In the wake of their elimination, The California Post graded the season of every player on the Dodgers’ roster.
First up, the offense, which ranked top-five in the regular season in scoring, batting average and OPS –– but faltered in the playoffs and was shut down in the NLCS.
Shohei Ohtani: F
To be clear: The two-way star was the second-best player in the National League this year, hitting 30 home runs and posting a sub-2.00 ERA in 14 starts on the mound. Even in a relatively down year for him, he finished fifth in the majors in Fangraphs’ version of wins above replacement. He remains, undoubtedly, MLB’s foremost star player and the Dodgers’ most potent weapon.
But that is why the way his season finished was such a failure.
What mattered most for the Dodgers this year was having Ohtani –– especially as a hitter –– at full strength come the postseason. By trying to play through right arm and left knee injuries, he wasn’t.
And while there is blame to be shared for the way his health was managed, from team decision-makers to Ohtani himself, it is impossible not to second-guess what this October might have looked like if the slugger was in a better place physically.
Instead, his .192 playoff batting average was not nearly enough to save the Dodgers’ offense. In the end, his one big swing in Game 4 of the NLCS was too little, too late. Moving forward, he and the team might have to reimagine his usage to avoid a repeat of this year. Because, especially as the rest of the roster gets older, they can’t afford another late-season injury crisis like this with Ohtani again.
Freddie Freeman: B-
In his 17th MLB season, Freeman earned his 10th career All-Star selection, finished 13th in the majors in total hits, and continued his march towards Cooperstown. But, the 37-year-old also saw his total production (measured by WAR) decline for a fourth-straight year.
He hit just one regular-season home run after July 4. His batting average dropped from .306 to .288 amid a knee issue in September. And despite a couple big swings in the playoffs, he finished October just 5-for-29. Now, entering the final season of his contract but intending to play at least a couple more beyond that, the Dodgers will have to start deciding if he will remain in their longer-term plans.
Mookie Betts: B
What was shaping up to be a lost year for Betts instead finished with signs of renewed life. On Aug. 4, he was hitting .223 with a .670 OPS. In 46 games after that, he posted a .315/.399/.562 slash line while nearly doubling his home run total from 13 to 23.
It was the best he had looked since the first half of 2024 and a reminder that, even at 34 years old now, there is a superstar level he is still capable of reaching. The Dodgers will be hoping that’s what they get from him in 2027.
Max Muncy: B+
This was a resurgent season for Muncy, who returned to the All-Star Game for the first time since 2021 while hitting for his highest average (.252) since 2018. He stayed healthy, playing 149 games and hitting 29 home runs.
He also improved his defense, earning a nod as a Gold Glove finalist at third base. He’ll be back at third next season, in the final guaranteed year of his contract.
Andy Pages: A-
Pages didn’t sustain his torrid pace from early in the year (he had a .303 average and .899 OPS on May 27, then a .254 average and .751 OPS thereafter) but still cemented himself as the youngest core piece of the roster, earning an All-Star nod with his improved approach and stellar center-field defense. His postseason was an improvement from 2025 too.
Teoscar Hernández: C
A late surge at the plate helped save some of Hernández’s season-long numbers (.267 average, .759 OPS) following a prolonged slump upon his return from a hamstring strain.
But after being bandied around in potential trade discussions last offseason, it’s possible his future with the club could be in question again this winter.
Kyle Tucker: D
The only thing saving this from being an F is the way Tucker finished his otherwise dismal debut season, highlighted by a team-best .333 batting average in the playoffs. Still, the 29-year-old played nowhere near expectations after his $240 offseason signing, setting career-lows in average (.233), OPS (.715) and home runs (17).
The Dodgers will be desperate for him to return to form next year, when he will play an even more vital role in their still-aging lineup. If not, those $60 million player options in 2028 and 2029 will start to feel like poison pills.
Will Smith: C
This is a relatively incomplete grade, given Smith was limited to just 73 games by a three-month neck injury. But even when he did play, the veteran backstop took a step back. His .260 average and .781 OPS were the second-lowest marks of his career (ahead of only 2024). He went just 3-for-31 in the playoffs, salvaging only so much with his Game 3 double in the NLCS.
Tommy Edman: C
After missing the start of the year recovering from ankle surgery, Edman did little more than meet expectations in his utility role with the Dodgers. He was a streaky .247 hitter, finishing with a just-about-league-average .714 OPS. He played good defense and shifted around the diamond. But any more profound impact was limited.
Kiké Hernández: C
Injuries derailed Hernández’s year. And though he had another big October moment –– hitting a home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS –– there was little else to take from his 13th big-league campaign. Once again a free agent, he will represent one of the more intriguing questions of the Dodgers’ winter.
Each of the last three offseasons, they have re-signed him to a one-year deal. Whether they do so again could be a signal for how much, or little, of a shake-up they’re planning for next year.
Dalton Rushing: B
For Rushing, it was a year of promising highs (seven home runs in March/April, .288 batting average in July) and frustrating lows (emotional outbursts early in the year, his spat with Ohtani on the mound in June, and a late-season elbow injury that sidelined him for the playoffs) for the former top prospect. He has more to prove entering Year 3 in 2027.
Alex Freeland: C
Another ex-prospect, Freeland didn’t capitalize on increased opportunity this year, hitting just .234 with only 13 extra-base hits in 89 games. Though still only 25, he remains on the fringes of the team’s long-term plans.
Alex Call: C
The backup outfielder survived the trade deadline. But after hitting just .233 in his reserve role, he might not be a lock to return in his reserve role next year.
Josue De Paula: B+
In his brief MLB debut, De Paula did everything right as a hitter, reaching base at a .500 clip in 11 regular-season games before drawing two key walks as a pinch-hitter in October. Offensively, he seems ready for everyday big-league duties. But the gigantic question mark about his outfield defense leaves his 2027 role unclear entering the winter.
Hyeseong Kim: D
Time will tell if the Dodgers still see something in Kim. But the way he was buried in triple-A this year, after playing just 43 games in the majors in April and May, was not a good sign as he enters the final guaranteed year of his contract.
Hunter Feduccia: B
The former Dodgers farmhand returned to the club in a deadline day trade and was perfectly adequate as the backup catcher over the final couple months of the season. Whether there’s a role for him in the organization again next year remains to be seen.
Miguel Rojas: A
We’re grading on a curve here, in what was a fittingly effective send-off season for the now-retired veteran infielder. Rojas did his job by menacing left-handed pitching (.293 average against them), playing stout defense and serving as a vocal leader in the Dodgers’ star-studded clubhouse. After an accomplished 13-year MLB career –– highlighted by his season-saving home run in Game 7 of last year’s World Series –– his presence will be missed in the clubhouse.

item.title: [Jays Journal] Dodgers' Miguel Rojas, who stole World Series away from Blue Jays, retires
item.dc:creator: Edward Eng

item.content:encoded:
With one swing of the bat in the ninth inning of Game 7, Miguel Rojas cemented himself in LA Dodgers history. Rojas took a pitch from Toronto Blue Jays closer Jeff Hoffman over the fence in left field to tie the series finale at 4-4. It sent shockwaves around Rogers Centre and Blue Jays fans everywhere felt the championship starting to slip away.
After that blast he would further draw the ire of Blue Jays fans when his throw cut down Isiah Kiner-Falefa at the plate in the bottom of the ninth, which prevented him from scoring the winning run. You know the rest of the story. The Dodgers won in extra innings, their second straight title, while Toronto havent' won it all in over three decades.
Rojas played hero for the Dodgers that night and after LA was eliminated from this year's NLCS, Rojas has officially called it a career. Rojas announced the previous year that he intended to retire following the 2026 campaign and he was certainly true to his word.
Miguel Rojas retires from professional baseball with two World Series rings in his collection
That concludes a 13-year major league career that saw him play for only two teams in the big leagues with the Dodgers and Miami Marlins. He began his pro-ball career with the Cincinnati Reds signing as an amateur free agent out of Venezuela in 2006.
In 2012 the Dodgers signed him to a minor league contract and he made his MLB debut in June of 2014. He was then part of a trade that winter that sent 2B Dee Gordon and RHP Dan Haren to the Marlins in exchange for LHP Andrew Heaney, RHP Chris Hatcher, 2B Enrique Hernandez and C Austin Barnes.
He spent the next eight seasons with the Marlins before he was traded back to LA in exchange for SS Jacob Amaya.
Over his career, Rojas compiled a .260 batting average, .677 OPS, along with 457 runs scored, 210 doubles, 11 triples, 61 home runs, 386 RBIs and 68 stolen bases in 1401 career MLB games played. This year in his final season of his baseball career, he posted a .267/.312/.391/.703 slash line, together with 23 runs scored, 16 doubles, four home runs and 23 RBIs in 105 games with Los Angeles.
Rojas may not have collected any personal hardware during his time in the leagues, but he certainly played a role in the Dodgers’ back-to-back World Series wins in 2024 and 2025. He also only hit 61 total dingers for his career, but none was bigger than the lone home run in the ninth on the night of Nov. 1, 2025. That moment alone solidifies him in LA Dodgers lore.

item.title: [dailybulletin.com] Analysis: Dodgers’ NLCS defeat raises questions about team’s aging core
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
