After their four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series at the hands of a younger, hungrier Milwaukee Brewers team ended the dream of a ‘three-peat,’ how realistic is it to head into 2027 with the same core – the oldest position player group in MLB for the past four years? “That’s not my job. I play first base,” said Freddie Freeman, at 37 the oldest returning p
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The past two years, the Dodgers’ season ended with parades and calls to “Run it back” for the next season.
After their four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series at the hands of a younger, hungrier Milwaukee Brewers team ended the dream of a ‘three-peat,’ how realistic is it to head into 2027 with the same core – the oldest position player group in MLB for the past four years?
“That’s not my job. I play first base,” said Freddie Freeman, at 37 the oldest returning player on the Dodgers’ roster (infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement and relief pitcher Blake Treinen, who suffered a shoulder injury late in the season, is a free agent).
“We’ve got a great group of guys. We’ve accomplished a lot of things. We came up short in these four days. But we’ll see where the wind blows this offseason, what happens, what it looks like, what baseball looks like.”
The winds of change could be coming. As Freeman alluded to, the anticipated showdown between MLB’s owners and the players’ union over the next Collective Bargaining Agreement could force the biggest changes in the Dodgers’ future. If the owners are able to get the salary cap or other payroll restrictions they are aiming for, the Dodgers might be forced to change their roster by shedding payroll.
Also looming over the team’s future are the ongoing legal and financial difficulties surrounding principal owner Mark Walter that threaten to eat into the Dodgers’ enormous financial advantages.
Threatening the franchise’s plans to keep its “Golden Era” going more directly, though, is the aging roster. The Brewers certainly made the Dodgers look old in the four-game NLCS sweep.
“I don’t know what you can really say to that. That’s just people’s opinions of what that is,” Freeman said before Game 4. “We do know we have an older team. That doesn’t mean we’re old and we’re playing bad because we’re old. We’re just not playing that great, in my mind.
“But that’s people’s opinions. I can’t change your opinion because we are, in this game, a little bit older than everybody else. I don’t feel old.”
Nonetheless, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman acknowledged awareness – if not overt concern – about the aging core on the team’s roster.
“Yeah, we’ve talked about this a lot,” Friedman said before the start of the NLCS. “With where we are in the success cycle, the success we have had, we have done the opposite of being flippant about it. ‘Oh, it’s great that we won. Now we can put our feet up.’ For us, it’s about pressing the advantage we have right now.
“We have a very talented core, and while a good number of them are getting up there in years, the experience, the way they prepare, the way they play the game, we feel like is a real competitive advantage. So we’ve been aggressive to supplement around that group, all the while pouring ourselves into our next wave.”
The Dodgers’ farm system is indeed as strong as any in MLB. They subtracted two Top 100 prospects (outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-hander River Ryan) in order to trade for pitcher Tarik Skubal in August and still have five more led by outfielder Josue De Paula.
De Paula made the jump from Double-A to the majors in September and showed his readiness in that brief audition. The Dodgers will have to make room for him in their 2027 plan.
That won’t be easy and it’s difficult to see how the Dodgers can get younger in 2027 other than around the margins where Kiké Hernandez acknowledged Game 4 of the NLCS might be his last with the Dodgers and Rojas made it clear, talking to the team after the game and saying he was retiring. He is expected to stay with the organization in some capacity, likely in player development.
“This is it as a player. That was my last game playing. That was the last time I put these cleats on and this uniform on as a player,” Rojas said, still in full uniform long after the game ended Thursday night. “From now on, I’m going to start thinking about what’s going to happen in my life as a baseball person other than being a player. I want to start my career on the other side of this business, and I’m looking forward to doing it here with the Los Angeles Dodgers as well.
“I’m ready to move on and start the next chapter of my career.”
Hernandez isn’t ready to stop playing. But he knows it might not be in Los Angeles next year.
“I mean, I love this place. I’ve played for three other teams, but every time I look at my career I kind of obviously go back to this place,” the 35-year-old Hernandez said. “I feel like I have a lot left. … I would love to be back. I would love to have one more try, trying to win another one. But I don’t really know what’s going to happen. I hope I’m back, and if I’m not I hope that I get to play for a winning team.”
Seven other Dodgers will become free agents this winter, most prominently bullpen stalwarts Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips and Skubal. Four others – Freeman, outfielder Teoscar Hernandez, third baseman Max Muncy and utility player Hyeseong Kim – are entering the final year of their contracts in 2027, though all but Freeman have club options for 2028.
If the Dodgers are going to change things by their own hand (as opposed to CBA mandate), Teoscar Hernandez clearly has a target on his back as the most likely Dodger to be traded this winter, clearing left field for De Paula. But the Dodgers have largely painted themselves into a corner with this roster. Freeman, shortstop Mookie Betts, catcher Will Smith, center fielder Andy Pages, right fielder Kyle Tucker, two-way star Shohei Ohtani and Muncy, each a year older, are all likely to be in the starting lineup on Opening Day 2027 – whenever that might be.
“I have no idea,” Muncy said of the potential for changes before next season. “That’s for people above me to make those decisions and it’s for me to show up next year, ready to go with whatever group we’ve got. There will come a time when we think about next year. But that’s not at this moment.”
Showing up at Camelback Ranch next spring with the same core is not necessarily a bad thing. Even with only minimal changes, the Dodgers will enter 2027 as the favorites in the National League West once again and a 15th consecutive postseason berth would bring another chance to win the “crapshoot” October has become.
But it also brings this Dodger core closer to “the cliff” Friedman has talked about avoiding.
“It’s tricky because you have to find the right balance,” he said. “It’s hard to transition young players onto your roster. It’s a hard adjustment from Triple-A to the major-league level. We’ve done it some over the years. Some guys we haven’t had the patience long enough to kind of see it through (perhaps an allusion to infielder Miguel Vargas, now an All-Star for the Chicago White Sox).
“That’s the challenge we have with the expectations we have. So we have to be mindful of having a really high standard but also transitioning some of our young players. We’ve seen it some, Andy Pages is featured prominently for us, Will Smith, Alex Freeland got a lot of opportunities this year. Dalton Rushing was a big part when Will missed time. And then late in the year we saw with Josue De Paula.
“We’ve got a lot of guys coming after that as well. So for us it’s about almost having a split personality – to do everything we can to maximize our chances of winning with our major-league roster, and the other side of our personality is pouring ourselves into doing everything we can to have as much talent coming, and we feel really good about that part as well.”

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers will have a new look in 2027.
Yes, Shohei Ohtani and Mookie Betts will still be in the lineup, but the roster will likely feature a much different set of faces than the 2026 group of Dodgers. One player that won’t be back with the team is Miguel Rojas, who confirmed NLCS Game 4 was the final game of his career.
The veteran infielder took to social media to thank his teammates for the wonderful journey he’s been on since his return to LA in 2023.
“All I can say is THANK YOU for changing my life 💙,” Rojas said.
“I will forever be grateful and so proud that I wore Dodger blue and represented this community every single day.

“Love you Dodger Family .-
“Miggy Ro 🫡.”
Rojas made his Major League debut with the Dodgers in 2014, but was traded to Miami ahead of the 2015 season. He was re-acquired by LA in 2023, a season before the Dodgers went on to win the first of their back-to-back World Series.
Rojas was a central piece to the Dodgers’ curation of a tight-knit clubhouse. The 37-year-old was viewed as a leader of the team and praised for his defensive prowess as an experienced infielder. Rojas etched his name into Dodgers postseason history when he hit the game-tying home run in the ninth inning of World Series Game 7 against the Blue Jays.
While Rojas won’t be on the Dodgers roster next season, the culture he helped build remains.

item.title: [aol.com] Shohei Ohtani's health and a possible lockout loom over an uncertain offseason for the Dodgers - AOL

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year.
Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break.
Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss to the Brewers that completed Milwaukee's sweep of the NL Championship Series. If he does, would the recovery bleed into the start of next season?
A potential MLB lockout is looming with the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. Team owners have proposed a salary cap — something the sport has never had — and the players' union has adamantly rejected the idea.
A work stoppage would give Ohtani extra time to heal, although during such time the Dodgers would be cut off from communicating with any player, leaving Ohtani to rehab either from possible surgery or from his injuries on his own.
Communication between Ohtani and the team on his health during the season was “awesome,” Andrew Friedman, president of baseball operations, said last month, but he added: “The fully sharing exactly how he's feeling, maybe not so awesome.”
Ohtani said he plans to resume pitching next year, when he'll turn 33 in July. He's already had two Tommy John surgeries.
“What he’s doing is unprecedented, and it takes a real toll,” Friedman said. “And as you get older, I think us just being very dialed is going to be really important.”
Roster turnover is likely, even without big changes in MLB spending rules
The Dodgers had baseball's second-highest opening day payroll this year at $323.3 million, behind the New York Mets at $358.4 million. If a salary cap were to be imposed, the Dodgers' spending would be constrained when play resumes.
Some of the roster could look different next year, too, with nine players set to become free agents after the World Series, led by two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is expected to command a huge deal.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal from Detroit just before the trade deadline in August. The left-hander was 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 regular-season games for his new team. In the postseason, he was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA and 14 Ks. Skubal didn't want to discuss his future Thursday, although he expressed enthusiasm for the organization, his teammates and the fans.
Advertisement
Other impending free agents are infielder Miguel Rojas, utility player Kiké Hernández, and relievers Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Blake Treinen and Alex Vesia.
As expected, Rojas announced his retirement Thursday, saying, “This is it, guys. That was my last game played.” He'll still be around, though, to work in a player development role.
Dodgers add a bit of youth with De Paula
The Dodgers got a glimpse of the future when they promoted Josue De Paula directly from Double-A to the majors in September. His energy and at-bats at designated hitter during Ohtani's stint on the injured list made an impression, and the 21-year-old was added to the postseason roster as a pinch-hitter.
The team will look to De Paula to further improve as an outfielder in 2027, although finding playing time for him will be challenging given the trio of veteran starters: Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker. De Paula is also blocked at DH by Ohtani.
“I think the experience he got being up here and watching what our guys do on a daily basis just helped connect some dots for him,” Friedman said. “And so, physically, he is capable of being a good corner outfielder, and we’re going to continue to tap into that.”
Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Ohtani, Tucker, Max Muncy and Will Smith will remain the Dodgers' veteran core. But some supporting players could be offloaded, like Kiké Hernández. Playing on a one-year deal, the 35-year-old was limited to 41 games while recovering from injuries and he didn't provide his usual postseason pop.
Manager Dave Roberts refused to blame an aging lineup for getting swept by the Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were three more than the Dodgers.
“We got beat,” he said. “There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested.”
There's drama off the field, too.
Owner Mark Walter was noticeably absent from the team's playoff games. He is facing multiple federal investigations into his business empire for possible financial improprieties involving insurance companies he controls. Walter has denied any wrongdoing. Since August, he sold his controlling interest in the Los Angeles Lakers and last month he unloaded his share in Chelsea of the Premier League.
___

item.content:encoded:
El out final que entregó Enrique «Kike» Hernández este jueves marcó el cierre de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional —en la que los Cerveceros de Milwaukee barrieron en cuatro juegos a los Dodgers de Los Ángeles— y, al mismo tiempo, detonó un momento inolvidable para el venezolano Miguel Rojas.
Ese instante marcó formalmente la conclusión de su trayectoria sobre el terreno de juego. Si bien el jugador de cuadro (infielder) de 37 años admitió previo al arranque de la serie que no mantenía el retiro en mente de forma activa, también aclaró que definiría su futuro una vez concluida la campaña del equipo californiano.
Y el momento del adiós se concretó en el propio vestuario del conjunto angelino.
«Hasta aquí llego, este es el final de mi etapa como pelotero», declaró conmovido tras culminar el compromiso. «Deseo que me recuerden como un profesional que dio absolutamente todo por el éxito de sus compañeros y por el crecimiento diario del grupo; me voy sumamente orgulloso de eso».
A lo largo de sus 11 temporadas en las Grandes Ligas, Rojas se caracterizó por ser un pilar defensivo y un líder positivo dentro del clubhouse, ganándose el respeto de compañeros, técnicos y aficionados tanto en Miami como en Los Ángeles.
El impacto de su entrega fue innegable durante su estadía en el equipo californiano. Resulta imposible concebir el bicampeonato de los Dodgers sin aquel memorable batazo de cuatro esquinas que conectó en el noveno capítulo del Juego 7 de la Serie Mundial, respaldado por un par de engalanadas joyas defensivas en las entradas finales.
Noticias Venevision / MLB. com

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Mookie Betts Reflects on "Our Leader," Miguel Rojas
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Mookie Betts struggled to find the words for what Miguel Rojas had meant to him. After the Dodgers’ season ended and Rojas confirmed his retirement, Betts described a teammate whose steady guidance had helped him grow on the field. “I don’t even have words to really describe him, especially for me and all the growth that I’ve had from him,” Betts said. “It’s kind of like that dad kind of sitting over and watching, making sure I’m good, making sure I’m learning everything.” “Eve
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Mookie Betts struggled to find the words for what Miguel Rojas had meant to him. After the Dodgers’ season ended and Rojas confirmed his retirement, Betts described a teammate whose steady guidance had helped him grow on the field.
“I don’t even have words to really describe him, especially for me and all the growth that I’ve had from him,” Betts said. “It’s kind of like that dad kind of sitting over and watching, making sure I’m good, making sure I’m learning everything.”
“Even to this game, every game I took the field, he was always there watching and making sure I’m doing everything right.”
A Leader Who Held Everyone Accountable
Rojas’ influence reached well beyond his work with Betts. In a clubhouse filled with stars and seasoned players, he had become a voice the whole team counted on.
“For the boys, he’s just kind of like our leader, you know?” Betts said. “He’s our vocal guy. He gets on the mic, makes sure we’re playing the game hard, holds everybody accountable.”
“Not having him in a uniform will be something completely different for all of us.”
That tribute spoke to the gap Rojas will leave behind. His teammates relied on him for the daily work of keeping a club sharp, from watching the details on the field to speaking up when something needed to be said.
A Season That Took the Whole Roster
The Dodgers reached the NLCS through injuries, slumps and stretches that called on players throughout the organization to help. Betts saw that run as a sign of how much the group believed in one another.
“It’s how much we care about each other,” he said. “And knowing that, hey, somebody’s hurt, we’ve got to step up, even the young guys coming in and stepping up.”
“I think it just shows the camaraderie and the belief that we have in each other.”
For the healthy players, that meant holding things together while injured teammates worked toward a return.
“We had some injuries, but we knew that those guys were grinding to get back,” Betts said. “We had to figure out our way to take care of business until they got back.”
“Baseball’s not played with just the 26 guys. It’s played with the whole roster, and sometimes more. So we have a beautiful thing here with a lot of guys that play the game really well.”
Winning Comes With No Guarantees
Betts also faced a question about whether another team winning might be good for baseball, given how much of the sport had come to view the Dodgers as the enemy. He quickly pointed out the bind in being asked to welcome someone else’s success after his own season had ended.
“That’s a damned if you do, damned if you don’t question you just asked,” Betts said.
“Whoever wins, wins. Of course I would love to win every time, but it’s not really built that way.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
Miguel Rojas puso punto final a su carrera como jugador de Grandes Ligas después de que los Los Angeles Dodgers quedaron eliminados por los Milwaukee Brewers en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional.
El pelotero venezolano anunció su retiro la noche del jueves, luego de 13 años en las Mayores, en un momento emotivo que compartió con sus compañeros en los vestuarios.
“Ha llegado el momento, muchachos. Ha llegado el momento”, expresó Rojas ante los periodistas. El infielder reconoció que había llegado la hora de comenzar una nueva etapa en su vida y en el béisbol, luego de disputar su último encuentro con el uniforme de los Dodgers.
“Hoy fue la última vez que me puse este uniforme como jugador, así como mis zapatillas de béisbol. Resulta muy difícil quitármelas en este momento”, manifestó el venezolano.
Sin embargo, su despedida como jugador no significa necesariamente un adiós definitivo a la organización angelina. Rojas dejó claro que desea continuar ligado al equipo desde otra función y contribuir a su desarrollo.
“Quiero ser leal, quiero seguir aquí, seguir vistiendo este uniforme y este logo, desde una capacidad diferente, y seguir mejorando la organización”, agregó.
Una carrera ligada a los Dodgers
Rojas llegó a los Dodgers por primera vez en 2014, pero en diciembre de ese mismo año fue canjeado a los Miami Marlins. Su regreso a Los Ángeles se concretó en 2023, lo que le permitió continuar su trayectoria con una organización con la que alcanzaría momentos importantes.
Uno de los capítulos más destacados de su carrera llegó en la Serie Mundial de 2025, cuando conectó un cuadrangular en el Juego 7 frente a los Toronto Blue Jays. Su batazo permitió que el encuentro continuara a entradas extra, instancia en la que los Dodgers consiguieron la victoria y celebraron su segundo campeonato consecutivo.
A sus 37 años, Rojas se despide del terreno de juego con dos títulos de Serie Mundial y una trayectoria de 1,401 partidos disputados en las Grandes Ligas.
El venezolano concluyó su carrera con una línea ofensiva de .260 de promedio de bateo, .313 de porcentaje de embasado y .363 de slugging, cifras que acompañan el cierre de una etapa de 13 temporadas en el mejor béisbol del mundo.
Ahora, tras la eliminación de los Dodgers ante Milwaukee, Rojas inicia el camino hacia una nueva etapa, con la intención de permanecer cerca del equipo y seguir aportando a la organización desde otro lugar.

item.title: [finchannel] Miguel Rojas retires after Dodgers’ NLCS exit, with plans to remain in baseball - FINCHANNEL

Speaking to reporters at Dodger Stadium, Rojas confirmed that his playing career was over. True Blue LA reported that he wanted to stay with the Dodgers, with an anti
item.content:encoded:
Miguel Rojas retired Thursday, October 15, at 37 after the Los Angeles Dodgers’ elimination from the National League Championship Series. The infielder’s final game ended with Milwaukee completing a four-game sweep, leaving him to discuss a planned move into another role with the organization where he began his major league career.
Speaking to reporters at Dodger Stadium, Rojas confirmed that his playing career was over. True Blue LA reported that he wanted to stay with the Dodgers, with an anticipated emphasis on player development, although the precise role remained undetermined. His retirement was also reported by MLB.com, the Los Angeles Times and Fox’s OutKick.
Rojas finished after 13 major league seasons split between Los Angeles and the Miami Marlins. His second Dodgers stint included two World Series championships and the home run that tied Game 7 of the 2025 championship against Toronto. He returned for one final season in 2026 after signing a one-year, $5.5 million contract.
A final game without a plate appearance
Rojas played two innings at second base in Thursday’s finale but did not bat, according to True Blue LA’s account. His final two major league plate appearances had come in Game 3 on Wednesday, when he singled and walked. All seven of his plate appearances in this postseason came against left-handed pitching.
The account listed a double alongside that single and walk in his final postseason. During the 2026 regular season, he hit .293 against left-handers, with a .340 on-base percentage and .469 slugging percentage. Those figures describe his production against left-handed pitchers, rather than his overall season.
MLB’s regular-season figures show that Rojas hit .267 with four home runs and 23 runs batted in during 2026.
The Dodgers’ season ended in a 6-4 loss after they had built a four-run lead. Shohei Ohtani supplied a three-run homer in the second inning off Dustin May. Milwaukee erased the advantage by the fifth, then moved ahead on Garrett Mitchell’s sixth-inning home run against Tanner Scott.
David Hamilton added a ninth-inning solo homer. Aaron Ashby completed a three-inning save, closing a game in which Los Angeles had doubles in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings without scoring those runners. The Dodgers went 2 for 11 with runners in scoring position Thursday.
The Brewers advanced to their first World Series since 1982 and their first as a National League club. For Los Angeles, the defeat ended the pursuit of a third consecutive championship. Rojas addressed his teammates after manager Dave Roberts’s postgame meeting, according to MLB.com’s account of the clubhouse.
Returning for the last season
The decision followed a plan Rojas had discussed before the 2026 season. MLB.com’s December 2025 report on his new contract said he intended the coming year to be his last. The deal kept him in Los Angeles after an October in which he had rarely started before the final two World Series games.
True Blue LA’s report on that contract described a 2025 regular season in which he batted .262 with a .318 on-base percentage and .397 slugging percentage. He started more often at second and third base than at shortstop, the position he had played regularly earlier in his career.
His October assignment changed in Toronto. Rojas started at second base in Games 6 and 7 after starting only twice in the Dodgers’ first 15 postseason games. In Game 6, he handled the throw from left fielder Kiké Hernández to complete the double play that ended the game.
In Game 7, his solo homer with one out in the ninth tied the score. He also fielded a grounder in the bottom of that inning and threw home to prevent Toronto from scoring the winning run. The Dodgers subsequently won in extra innings.
A return trade and a changing infield role
Rojas made his Dodgers debut in 2014 before being traded to Miami that December in the larger deal involving Dee Gordon. He spent eight seasons with the Marlins, then returned to Los Angeles in January 2023 in exchange for shortstop Jake Amaya.
In eight of his first nine major league seasons, Rojas played for manager Don Mattingly. That stretch included his 2014 Dodgers debut and years in Miami, where he established himself as a regular shortstop.
The January 2023 account of the trade described a player whose defensive record offered Los Angeles experienced depth. Rojas had batted .236 in 2022, with a .283 on-base percentage and .323 slugging percentage. That season he tied Houston’s Jeremy Peña for the most Defensive Runs Saved among major league shortstops, with 15, according to the report.
He had been a National League Gold Glove finalist at shortstop in both 2020 and 2022. The Dodgers acquired him as Gavin Lux was preparing to take on a larger role at the position. Rojas also brought experience at third base and second base, giving the team alternatives across the infield.
Lux’s spring-training knee injury subsequently changed the arrangement. In a May 2024 report, True Blue LA recalled that Rojas had started 109 games during the previous season. In spring 2024, Mookie Betts was moving into an everyday shortstop role, with Rojas among those helping him make the transition.
Mentorship alongside the playing time
Roberts publicly credited Rojas, along with coaches Dino Ebel and Chris Woodward, for the work Betts had put into shortstop in 2024. The veteran’s assistance also included pregame drills and conversations during games, according to Eric Stephen’s reporting for True Blue LA.
That report described Rojas helping Lux return to second base and working with Miguel Vargas when Vargas was learning the position in 2023. Rojas invited Vargas to work out with him in Florida after being acquired by the Dodgers. He told the outlet that coaching was part of his ambition after his playing days.
In that 2024 interview, Rojas recalled Adrián González helping him as a rookie, including conversations about baseball and professional life off the field.
Three consecutive clubhouse awards
The recognition from teammates and coaches continued in September, when Rojas was voted the Dodgers’ Roy Campanella Award winner for 2026. The award honors the player judged to embody the Hall of Fame catcher’s leadership and spirit. Rojas had also won in 2024 and 2025.
According to the September account of the award, he became the first Dodger to receive it in three consecutive seasons. Justin Turner was the only other three-time recipient, with wins in 2017, 2019 and 2020.
Clayton Kershaw and Chase Utley had each won twice. Kershaw received the honor in 2013 and 2014, and Utley in 2016 and 2018.
The same report noted that Rojas had started games at second base, shortstop and third base during 2026 and had also played three innings at first. It described his plans to join the organization’s front office with a focus on developing players. Thursday’s retirement account left the precise assignment open.
Questions and answers
Did Rojas play for teams other than the Dodgers?
Yes. He spent eight major league seasons with Miami between his two periods in Los Angeles.
Was retirement already part of his plan?
He had said before the 2026 season that it would be his last as a player.
Will he stay with the Dodgers?
Rojas said he wanted to remain with the organization. Reporting described a prospective player-development role, with its precise form still undetermined.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Miguel Rojas delivers emotional news to Dodgers clubhouse after NLCS
item.dc:creator: Matthew Moreno
item.description: When the Los Angeles Dodgers re-signed Miguel Rojas to a one-year contract it was with an expectation he would retire following the 2026 season and immediately join the front office. But Rojas began to soften on his retirement stance as the season progressed and suggested he would return in 2027 if the Dodgers completed a three-peat and were in position to again defend their title. But with that possibility ruled out following a Milwaukee Brewers sweep in the National League Championship Series,
item.content:encoded:
When the Los Angeles Dodgers re-signed Miguel Rojas to a one-year contract it was with an expectation he would retire following the 2026 season and immediately join the front office.
But Rojas began to soften on his retirement stance as the season progressed and suggested he would return in 2027 if the Dodgers completed a three-peat and were in position to again defend their title. But with that possibility ruled out following a Milwaukee Brewers sweep in the National League Championship Series, the 37-year-old closed the book on his playing career.
Miguel Rojas informs Dodgers of retirement decision
After manager Dave Roberts spoke to the clubhouse following their Game 4 loss, he turned the floor over to Rojas. He used that opportunity to thank teammates for all they’ve done and announced he was retiring.
“Now that everything is done it’s going to be really hard to take this uniform off and move on with my life,” Rojas said while speaking with media. He was still dressed in his uniform and cleats, and spoke with tears in his eyes.
“This is where I’ve been for the majority of my life. I spent 21 years in professional baseball and obviously the last four here in this clubhouse, putting this uniform on every single day has been a privilege and pleasure. It’s not the way I wanted to end it, because we always wanted to win the last game of the season. But in baseball nothing is guaranteed.”
Rojas made his MLB debut with the Dodgers in 2014 and returned to the organization in 2023.
“It’s really amazing when I think about what happened to me and my family the last few years,” he said. “I talked to the guys, it was really emotional after the game, and I told them I’m going to be loyal. I want to stay here and wear this uniform in a different capacity and continue to make the organization better. But this is it. This is it as a player.”
Primarily known as a strong defender, Rojas will forever be remembered for his game-tying home run in the ninth inning of Game 7 of the 2025 World Series. He also memorably saved Clayton Kershaw’s only no-hitter of his career with a terrific stop and throw at third base.

item.title: [fansided.com] These 5 Dodgers won't be back next year after three-peat bid crashes and burns
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers appeared poised to three-peat as World Series champions. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers appeared poised to three-peat as World Series champions. They loaded up after winning their second straight title, signing Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in free agency and trading for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline. All they had to do was get through a Milwaukee Brewers team they swept in last year's NLCS in order to appear in a World Series against either Tampa Bay or Cleveland, both of whom L.A. would be favored to take care of.
Instead, the Dodgers' incredible run was stymied by Milwaukee in an NLCS that can only be classified as embarrassing for L.A. The Dodgers could not get anything going offensively, and their vaunted rotation underwhelmed. Now, with their three-peat bid having been a failure, an important offseason is ahead. Will Tarik Skubal be back? That shouldn't be ruled out. These other players, though, almost certainly won't be back with the Dodgers seeking revenge in 2027 (if there even is a 2027 season).
INF Miguel Rojas
Why not start out with an easy one? Miguel Rojas has made it clear that he plans on retiring after the 2026 campaign. He can always change his mind, and he told Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times that he wouldn't play for another team, but with Rojas now 37 years old and with a pair of World Series wins on his resume, what more does he have to play for?
Rojas retiring would be a tough blow for the Dodgers, given the fact that he's still a solid bench piece, is an important clubhouse presence, and recorded one of the biggest and unlikeliest hits in MLB history when he tied Game 7 of the 2025 World Series with a home run, but it's hard to imagine Rojas sticking around for another year.
RHP Blake Treinen
Once upon a time, Blake Treinen was one of the best relievers in the sport. He saved 38 games for the Athletics in 2018, and had a pair of sub-2.00 ERA seasons for the Dodgers in 2021 and 2024. Unfortunately, Treinen has a 4.47 ERA in 68 appearances since the start of the 2025 campaign, and injuries have limited him to fewer than 40 outings in each of those years.
Treinen missed nearly three months of the 2026 campaign with elbow inflammation, didn't pitch all that great upon his return, and was placed on the IL with shoulder inflammation at the end of the regular season. Injuries have been a common theme for Treinen over the course of his career, and while he had always been good enough to keep around despite his missed time, now, at 38 years old, he isn't what he once was. It's hard to envision the Dodgers being eager to bring him back.
LHP Kris Bubic
The Dodgers bolstered their pitching depth by acquiring Kris Bubic at the trade deadline from the Kansas City Royals. Sure, Bubic was hurt at the time, which made the move a bit risky, but L.A. made this move with the postseason in mind. Well, while Bubic came through with five scoreless appearances in the regular season, he allowed a run in each of his postseason appearances, taking a loss in the NLDS against the Braves and blowing a rare lead the Dodgers had in Game 2 of the NLCS against the Brewers.
These rough outings aren't reason enough to not want to bring Bubic back, but odds are, the southpaw is going to want to start (he was rock-solid in that role with the Royals), and I'm not sold that the Dodgers will be eager to guarantee him a rotation spot, with Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow locked in if healthy, and guys like Justin Wrobleski, Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan still in the organization. Odds are, Bubic will earn a solidified rotation spot elsewhere.
LHP Eric Lauer
The Dodgers dealt with a slew of pitching injuries, and brought Eric Lauer in to give them needed depth. To his credit, Lauer pitched quite well in his 13 appearances (11 starts) for the Dodgers. In fact, He allowed three earned runs or fewer in nine of his 11 starts and allowed just one run in eight innings in two appearances as a bulk reliever. If it weren't for a couple of especially brutal starts, Lauer's numbers in L.A. would've wound up looking much better than they did.
With that being said, Lauer ended the year on the IL with left elbow inflammation and, as is the case with Bubic, is probably looking for more of a solidified role than the Dodgers would be willing to give him. He'd be a solid option to bring back in a swingman role, but it's likely that the 31-year-old will end up elsewhere.
OF Teoscar Hernandez
Here's the big one. Teoscar Hernandez is the only player on this list under contract for 2027, and he's been a staple in L.A. since the 2024 campaign. There're a couple of reasons why it makes sense to move him, though. First, he's simply not worth the $17 million he's owed in 2027 after the year he just had. He still mashes left-handed pitching, but he had a subpar .695 OPS against righties in the regular season and is a very poor defensive outfielder. It's hard to justify playing him regularly on a team trying to contend.
Second, and perhaps most importantly, the Dodgers need to find a spot for top prospect Josue De Paula to play regularly. The ideal spot for De Paula, an outstanding hitter whose defense leaves much to be desired, would be DH, but that's Shohei Ohtani's spot for the foreseeable future. Kyle Tucker is locked into right field given his absurd contract, and De Paula can't play center field (nor should the Dodgers be eager to move off of Andy Pages). That leaves left field, Hernandez's spot, as the position where De Paula seems likeliest to slot in.
The Dodgers can keep Hernandez around as a platoon partner for De Paula, but a trade could make sense. Hernandez was in rumors last offseason, and I wouldn't be surprised to see those resurface this winter.

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers’ Shohei Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for must-win Game 4

Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup. Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason. “J
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Desperate times call for … unexpected measures.
Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup.
Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason.
“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said. “I liked the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a little bit – obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”
Ohtani is just 4 for 22 (.182) in the postseason, but that hardly stands out in the unproductive lineup. Through the first three games of the NLCS, the Dodgers were hitting .165 (15 for 91) as a team with just two extra-base hits and no home runs. Only Mookie Betts (3 for 12) had more than two hits.
“I think getting back to what we’ve done all year and how it’s been going recently as far as on the offense, I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup,” said Roberts, who also started Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernandez against Brewers left-hander Shane Drohan.
PHILLY CONNECTION
Before re-signing Don Mattingly to a contract extension as manager, the Philadelphia Phillies reached out to two members of the Dodgers’ front office with Philly connections – Chase Utley and Raul Ibañez.
Neither would confirm the contact, but neither interviewed for the job. Both have teen-aged children and Utley acknowledged family takes priority over pursuing a managerial career at this point.
Ibañez, currently the Dodgers’ vice president of baseball development and special projects, has been approached about managing on other occasions but declined. Utley is a special assistant to Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman.
AWARDS SEASON
Despite his injuries and a prolonged slump, Ohtani is one of the National League finalists for the Hank Aaron Award given to the top offensive performer in MLB during the regular season. Ohtani finished the season with a .275 average, 30 home runs and an .889 OPS. Ohtani has won it the past three seasons (twice in the NL and once with the Angels in the American League).
The other finalists are CJ Abrams (Washington Nationals), Jake Bauers (Milwaukee Brewers), Pete Crow-Armstrong (Chicago Cubs), Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart (Cincinnati Reds), Matt Olson (Atlanta Braves), Kyle Schwarber (Philadelphia Phillies), Fernando Tatis Jr. (San Diego Padres) and Jordan Walker (St. Louis Cardinals).
Ohtani is also one of three finalists for the Players’ Choice Outstanding Player Award along with Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber.
Max Muncy and Andy Pages have been named finalists for Gold Glove awards at their positions. Muncy is a finalist at third base along with Alex Bregman (Cubs) and Javier Sanoja (Miami Marlins). Pages is a finalist in center field along with Crow-Armstrong and Michael Harris II (Braves).
The Gold Glove winners will be announced on ESPN on Nov. 1.
UP NEXT
NLCS Game 5 (if necessary): Brewers (RHP Jacob Misiorowski, 16-5, 1.80 ERA) at Dodgers (LHP Tarik Skubal, 12-7, 2.72 ERA), Friday, 6 p.m. FS1, 570 AM

item.title: [CBS Sports] Who's to blame for Dodgers' shocking NLCS loss vs. Brewers? Five places to point fingers
item.dc:creator: Mike Axisa
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year aft
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year after the Dodgers swept them in the 2025 NLCS.
Who is to blame for the Dodgers going four-and-out in the NLCS? There's plenty of blame to go around, so let's assign it, shall we?
1. The Brewers
Milwaukee continues to be baseball's best team
We have to start here. The Dodgers got swept in the NLCS because the Brewers outplayed them in every phase of the game. The Brewers got better starting pitching. Their bullpen was better. Their defense and baserunning were better. Their offense was better at both stringing together hits to build a rally and launching the ball out of the park. Pat Murphy out-managed Dave Roberts as well. You name it, and the Brewers did it better than the Dodgers this series.
"It's a pretty simple answer," Dodgers infielder Max Muncy said after Game 3. "We're playing like shit. They're playing great."
As much as we want to (and will) blame various Dodgers for the sweep, the single biggest reason they got swept is that the Brewers were simply the better team. They were the better team in the regular season based on their records (103-59 vs. 100-62) and run differentials (+214 vs. +201), and they certainly played like the better team in the NLCS. The better team doesn't always win a postseason series. In the NLCS though, the better team has played like the better team, period.
2. Shohei Ohtani
MLB's brightest star was greatly dimmed ... even with Game 4 homer
The biggest star on baseball's most star-laden team was not himself the last two months of the season. Shohei Ohtani played through knee and biceps injuries and had been so unproductive than Roberts said there would at least be a "conversation" about sitting Ohtani in Game 3. That didn't come to pass, and hey, Ohtani went 1 for 2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch in Game 3, and hit a home run in Game 4. The homer put the Dodgers up 4-0 on Thursday. The Dodgers didn't score again. The bottom line is Ohtani was a non-factor until it was too late. It's hard to win when your best player is this diminished.
Whenever a team loses in the postseason, the best player gets a disproportionate amount of the blame, and that applies to Ohtani this series. He's clearly not healthy, , and he's had multiple chances in the first three games to swing things in his team's favor, but couldn't do it. When the best player underperforms, he wears most of the blame. It has been the way of the world since the dawn of team sports.
3. Freddie Freeman
Normally clutch, Freeman has been the worst player in the series
Freddie Freeman, not Ohtani, was the worst player in the NLCS by both win probability added and championship probability added. He went 1 for 14 in the series and the one hit came in the first inning of Game 1. Freeman went 0 for 13 after his first NLCS at-bat and that 0 for 13 includes:
- Striking out after Mookie Betts worked a leadoff walk in the third inning of Game 1.
- Grounding into an inning-ending double play in the fifth inning of Game 1.
- Popping up to second on the first pitch to lead off the eighth inning of Game 1.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and no outs in the third inning of Game 2.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and one out in the third inning of Game 3.
- Grounding out with a runner on first and two outs in the fifth inning of Game 3.
That's an awful lot of empty at-bats in clutch situations for one of the best clutch hitters of this generation. Freeman had as many double plays as total bases (one each) in the NLCS, and his only RBI came on a sacrifice fly. You won't beat a team as good as the Brewers with sac flies. You need bigger swings from your best players and Freeman didn't provide them.
4. The supporting cast
Only two Dodgers hitters had consistently strong at-bats in the NLCS
Max Muncy went 2 for 12 with six strikeouts in the NLCS. Teoscar Hernández went 3 for 14. Andy Pages went 3 for 12. Tommy Edman went 1 for 7. Will Smith went 2 for 15 in the NLCS. Postseason legend Enrique Hernández went 0 for 8 with a ghasty strikeout in Game 3. The Dodgers had runners at second and third with one out in sixth, and Hernández took two pitches in the zone for strikes, then flailed at slider out of the zone. It was maybe the single worst at-bat of this NLCS.
Freeman was terrible, Ohtani was terrible, and the thing that has so often set the Dodgers apart these last few years -- an elite supporting cast -- was terrible as well. Edman, Muncy, Smith, and the Hernándezes are a combined 11 for 58 (.189) in the four games. Betts (3 for 15 with three walks) and Kyle Tucker (4 for 12 with three walks) were the only Dodgers hitters who escaped scrutiny. They were their most productive hitters and consistently had strong at-bats. Everyone else? 😴😴😴
5. Dave Roberts
Roberts did not push the right buttons
The manager can not swing the bat or throw the ball for his players, but he can put his team in the best position to succeed, and Roberts did not do that in the NLCS. Game 3, especially, was a managerial mess. Roberts burned the precocious Josue De Paula in the sixth inning when he sent him up to pinch-hit for Miguel Rojas with runners on second and third and one out, then immediately pinch-hit Enrique Hernández for De Paula when the Brewers brought in a lefty reliever.
De Paula is a rookie, I get that, but he has a track record of hitting lefties well in the minors. More accurately, he has a strong track record of making contact against lefties, which is what the Dodgers needed in that spot. A ball in play to get a run home. Instead, Roberts defaulted to the veteran Hernández, who struck out feebly. For all his career postseason success, Hernández went 1 for 14 this postseason, and a .190/.235/.317 hitter in his last 19 postseason games. Roberts never adjusted his priors.
The NLCS was a flashback to pre-2024 Roberts, when he too often showed too much faith in his veterans and had an unfortunate knack for sticking with starters too long. In 2024 and 2025, it all worked out, and Roberts looked like a genius. Those same mistakes, the ones he got away with the last two years, reared their ugly heads. The NLCS sweep is on the players, first and foremost. Roberts didn't play his cards well either. He's made things worse.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers face an offseason reckoning after stunning NLCS sweep
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: The home run shredded the October sky like a bolt of lightning. Shohei Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers’ bench. He threw his bat. He screamed. He punched the air. He screamed some more. With one furious swing, Ohtani unleashed months of pent-up frustration. His streak of 115 plate appearances without a home run was over. But this wasn’t a series-altering three-run home run. This was a last stand. The four-run lead the Dodgers built up in that stadium-rocking second inning didn’t endure. The Milw
item.content:encoded:
The home run shredded the October sky like a bolt of lightning.
Shohei Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers’ bench.
He threw his bat. He screamed. He punched the air. He screamed some more.
With one furious swing, Ohtani unleashed months of pent-up frustration.
His streak of 115 plate appearances without a home run was over.
But this wasn’t a series-altering three-run home run.
This was a last stand.
The four-run lead the Dodgers built up in that stadium-rocking second inning didn’t endure. The Milwaukee Brewers saw that it wouldn’t.
As they did throughout this National League Championship Series, the Brewers pressed and pressed and pressed. Little by little, the Dodgers gave in.
By the sixth inning, the Dodgers were behind. Three innings later, they were officially eliminated from the playoffs when Kiké Hernández flied out to left field against Aaron Ashby for the final out of a 6-4 defeat at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers didn’t just lose.
They were swept in four games by the same team they swept at this stage of the postseason last year.
Now, comes the hard part.
The Dodgers might be the second-best team in baseball behind the Brewers, but they can’t return with a similar roster next season and expect the results to be any different.
Farewells are in order.
Farewell to long-time Dodgers who will forever be known in these parts as World Series heroes.
Farewell to Ohtani hitting and pitching full-time.
With how the Dodgers were thumped by the Brewers, president of baseball operation Andrew Friedman has a clear directive.
Adjust – or else.
The Dodgers have the oldest team in the major leagues. First baseman Freddie Freeman and infielder Miguel Rojas are 37. Third baseman Max Muncy is 36 and utilityman Kiké Hernández is 35. Shortstop Mookie Betts and outfielder Teoscar Hernández are 34.
The problem is magnified by their prime-aged players, who are breaking down as if they are senior citizens.
Ohtani, 32, was obviously debilitated in the postseason, which explains why a former 50-homer player wasn’t a power threat for the majority of these playoffs.
Catcher Will Smith, 31, was sidelined for three months with a disc problem, which contributed to him being out of sorts in the batter’s box.
Utilityman Tommy Edman, also 31, is an All-Star-caliber player when healthy – but he often isn’t.
Kyle Tucker, 29, flat-out stunk for the majority of the first season of his four-year, $240-million contract.
What Friedman and others in the front office will have to decide in the coming weeks and months is how quickly and drastically they will turn over the roster.
The Dodgers shopped Teoscar Hernández last offseason, and they figure to do so again this offseason, as they already have a promising in-house replacement for him in left field in 21-year-old rookie Josue De Paula. Hernández has only one more guaranteed year remaining on his contract.
But what do the Dodgers do beyond that?
Do they attempt to move some of their other veterans? Or do they field more or less the same team next season, accept the limitations of their roster, and wait for some of their contracts to expire in another year?
Freeman will be an unrestricted free agent after the 2027 season. Muncy could also depart that winter, as his option for the 2028 season is a team option.
There are no simple answers.
Muncy’s option for 2028 is a relative bargain at $10 million, for example. The Dodgers might not be able to find a better third baseman at that price point.
Or, in the case of Freeman, how can they not re-sign a player as beloved as he is?
One factor that could influence the Dodgers’ team-building approach: Baseball’s next collective-bargaining agreement.
More restrictive spending limits of some kind figure to be on their way, as franchise owners are pushing for a salary cap. The Dodgers could be forced to dump salaries whether they want to or not.
Whatever happens on that front, the Dodgers will have to address Ohtani’s situation.
Ohtani broke into Japan’s top league as an 18 year old. He was a two-way player in the five seasons he played for the Nippon-Ham Fighters, and his body has plenty of mileage on it.
This season was particularly demanding.
Last year, resumed pitching in the middle of the season after recovering from his second major elbow operation. This year, he attempted to be a full-time hitter and pitcher for the entire season.
Ohtani broke down. He abandoned pitching in the middle of the season. The resulting injuries diminished him as a hitter.
Knowing Ohtani will insist on remaining a two-way player, what do the Dodgers do?
Do they spread out his starts to extend the periods between his starts? Or do they try to sell him on the idea that by not pitching in the early parts of the season, he could be a two-way player in October?
The results have spoken.
Changes will have to be made.

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] Brewers sweep Dodgers in NLCS to book ticket to World Series
item.dc:creator: Ben Nicholson-Smith
item.description: LOS ANGELES — With the score tied at four in the top of the sixth inning, Tanner Scott threw a fastball down the middle and Garrett Mitchell crushed it. As the ball soared over the centre field wall at Dodger Stadium, reality set in for the two-time defending champions and their fans: their reign atop MLB might be ending. And a few innings later, when Aaron Ashby retired Kiké Hernandez for the final out of a 6-4 win in Game 4 of the NLCS, it was all over. There were late chances to score Kyle Tu
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — With the score tied at four in the top of the sixth inning, Tanner Scott threw a fastball down the middle and Garrett Mitchell crushed it.
As the ball soared over the centre field wall at Dodger Stadium, reality set in for the two-time defending champions and their fans: their reign atop MLB might be ending. And a few innings later, when Aaron Ashby retired Kiké Hernandez for the final out of a 6-4 win in Game 4 of the NLCS, it was all over.
There were late chances to score Kyle Tucker from second and Will Smith from third, but in the end the Dodgers failed.
They’re a great team, but not the best team in baseball anymore, or even the best team in the National League. That honour goes to the Milwaukee Brewers, who secured the pennant with a sweep of the Dodgers thanks to Mitchell’s big swing, some tenacious rallies in the middle innings and impressive relief pitching.
The win overshadowed a dramatic home run from Shohei Ohtani and disappointed 49,104 fans still hoping for a third straight championship. Instead, it’s Milwaukee who will represent the National League in the World Series in a battle of small markets against either Cleveland or Tampa Bay.
All series, the Brewers outplayed the Dodgers. They hit more home runs, they played better defence and they pitched better. And really, that should come as no surprise. This team has reached the post-season eight of the last nine seasons, including each of the last four NL Central titles.
But still, the Dodgers are baseball’s preeminent team, so when Shohei Ohtani demolished a Dustin May cutter to give the Dodgers an early 4-0 lead, their path to victory seemed to open up again. As the ball soared into the right-field bleachers, Ohtani bounced backwards towards first base and yelled at his teammates in the third-base dugout. It may be the most emotion he’s ever shown on a big-league field.
Considering the context, Ohtani’s home run was all the more significant. Just two days ago, there was talk of benching him given his middling performance and knee and biceps injuries. Then came a stellar performance in Game 3 and his Game 4 home run, the first one he’s hit since August 18.
But aside from Ohtani’s big swing, the Dodgers simply didn’t have answers offensively. No one else homered in the NLCS. In fact, they had just five other extra-base hits this series — all doubles. A team known for its high-powered offence had produced backup-catcher type numbers when it counted most.
They needed to hit or see their season end, no in-between. And they didn’t hit, so their season ended.
The Brewers, on the other hand, managed just enough offence. David Hamilton added a late home run and breakout star Jake Bauers drove in three, including two with a pivotal double in the fourth inning. All series, they found answers against the Dodgers team that allowed the fewest runs in MLB this regular season.
Oddly enough, this will be the first time the Brewers represent the National League in the World Series. When they made it in 1982, they were still an American League team and lost to the Cardinals in seven games.
The Dodgers were seeking the first MLB three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees and only the fifth in MLB history (Athletics 1972-74; Yankees 1949-53; Yankees 1936-39). Instead, they’ll turn their attention to the off-season, with Hernandez, Miguel Rojas, Alex Vesia and, most notably, Tarik Skubal all headed for free agency.
Before then, the Brewers will participate in a World Series featuring two of MLB’s lowest payrolls, undermining the narrative that MLB needs a salary cap for small-market teams to compete. The Brewers didn’t just beat the Dodgers, they dominated them thanks to elite player acquisition, strong player development and a strong team culture.
Soon enough, more tests await the Brewers. First, though, it’s time for a well deserved celebration.

item.title: [FOX Sports] Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
item.description: Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4 One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. The Dodgers trailed the Milwaukee Brewers 3-0 in the best-of-seven series, and needed to four straight wins to reach the World Series and keep alive their bid for a third consecutive championship. Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night.
The Dodgers trailed the Milwaukee Brewers 3-0 in the best-of-seven series, and needed to four straight wins to reach the World Series and keep alive their bid for a third consecutive championship.
Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday night, the lowest he's hit since joining the Dodgers ahead of the 2024 season. He was 1 for 2 with a walk to raise his batting average to .182.
"Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at," manager Dave Roberts said before the game. "I liked the at-bats yesterday. Obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to."
(Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images)
Ohtani typically leads off the order but has been dropped lower while struggling with injuries to his left knee and right biceps for the last few months. Roberts didn't tell Ohtani about the change before posting the lineup.
Roberts said Ohtani has given him reasons to believe in the four-time MVP, citing Ohtani staying until 9 p.m. on Tuesday to work on his swing and his improved at-bat quality.
"Baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top," he said. "I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win and produce runs."
Roberts tweaked the entire lineup after Wednesday's loss put the Dodgers on the brink of elimination. Mookie Betts, who led off in Game 3, was bumped to No. 2, while Freddie Freeman moved to No. 3.
Will Smith, whose offensive struggles mirrored Ohtani's, moved up to fourth from seventh. Smith doubled in the sixth inning, when the Dodgers briefly took a 2-1 lead.
"I thought Will took very good at-bats, big hit yesterday," Roberts said. "He’s been in big spots."
Kyle Tucker hit fifth, while Teoscar Hernandez went from third to sixth. Miguel Rojas hit seventh and Andy Pages dropped to eighth from fifth.
Kiké Hernández, who came off the bench in Game 3, hit ninth, with regular third baseman Max Muncy available to come off the bench for Rojas or Kiké Hernández.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: [MLB.com] Back to basics: Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for NLCS Game 4
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- With their season on the line, the Dodgers are going back to their roots. Shohei Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for the first time this postseason as the Dodgers shook up their lineup ahead of Game 4 of the NL Championship Series against the Brewers on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium, a game they must win to keep their season -- and their three-peat bid -- alive. Ohtani dropped as low as sixth in the order in NLCS Game 3, when a scuffling Will Smith also dropped to seventh. Both
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- With their season on the line, the Dodgers are going back to their roots.
Shohei Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for the first time this postseason as the Dodgers shook up their lineup ahead of Game 4 of the NL Championship Series against the Brewers on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium, a game they must win to keep their season -- and their three-peat bid -- alive.
Ohtani dropped as low as sixth in the order in NLCS Game 3, when a scuffling Will Smith also dropped to seventh. Both contributed to the Dodgers' lone run-scoring rally in the sixth inning, with Ohtani drawing a walk to load the bases before Smith cashed in with a two-run double. Two innings later, Ohtani smoked a 113.5 mph single, his hardest-hit batted ball since June 20.
The big plate appearances from Ohtani and Smith, as well as the work they have put in behind the scenes, were enough to convince manager Dave Roberts to elevate both of them back up the order.
"I think getting back to what we've done all year and how it's been going recently as far as on the offense," Roberts said, "I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup."
Here's the full lineup:
1. Shohei Ohtani, DH
2. Mookie Betts, SS
3. Freddie Freeman, 1B
4. Will Smith, C
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernández, LF
7. Miguel Rojas, 2B
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Kiké Hernández, 3B
The Dodgers are trying to do what just one other team has done before: Come back from being down 0-3 in a best-of-seven postseason series. Of the 42 teams that have been in that position, only Roberts' 2004 Red Sox have successfully come back to win the series. Thirty-two of those series ended in sweeps.
Roberts' advice to his team is to focus solely on winning Game 4. They can't look at the big picture of needing four wins in as many games. They need to win each pitch, each inning and each day for as long as their season is alive.
Having Ohtani back atop the order, Roberts hopes, will put the Dodgers in the best position to do that. Ohtani is hitting 4-for-22 (.182) with no extra-base hits, seven strikeouts and four walks in seven games this postseason. There was a discussion about sitting him for Game 3 amid his lingering right biceps and left knee injuries, but Ohtani was adamant that he felt good enough to play and was close to figuring something out with his swing.
The reasoning for Ohtani's return to the leadoff spot a game later is twofold: He showed Roberts enough through his work and in Game 3. And if this is it for the Dodgers' postseason run, Roberts wants to go down trusting his generational talent to set the tone.
"There is something to that, absolutely," Roberts said. "But also I think the player still has to give you hope to believe in, to bet on -- where I think that the work, being here till 9 p.m. two nights ago working, the at-bats yesterday. For me baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top."

item.title: [si.com] Brewers Are Using Postseason Stage to Showcase MLB’s New Era
item.dc:creator: Tom Verducci
item.description: Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out. The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out.
The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Blake Snell on the mound with a lead and lost all three. Ninety-five million dollars, four Cy Young awards and a World Series MVP worth of pitching and they could not hold back Milwaukee any more than you can hold back water with your hands.
But the most obvious reason why the Brewers have put the Dodger dynasty on the brink of extinction is this: the youngest pitching staff in baseball—and the hardest throwing staff in postseason history—has smothered the oldest team in baseball. Milwaukee is pushing around the aging Dodgers lineup with a barrage of fastballs in three versions, especially power sinkers. They are shoving 66.8% fastballs at the Dodgers at an average velocity of 97.9 mph. The Dodgers’ only path to victory is to slug and the Brewers simply won’t allow it.
“I just think they’re really good pitchers,” Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard, and they’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too much of an opportunity to kind of build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They throw their stuff in the zone—and with all three fastballs. A lot of guys have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball. It’s really hard to put barrels on the ball.
“At the end of the day, it’s just the velocity of their stuff. They throw the ball really hard. And we all know when you throw that hard, it’s really hard.”
The Brewers knew coming into the series that in today’s game older players don’t hit elite fastballs as well as younger players, and so the matchup was to their liking. But this? Who could have seen this in the NLCS? The Dodgers:
- Have two extra-base hits in 105 plate appearances
- Have been outhomered, 5-0
- Are the first team in franchise history to lose three straight games in one postseason with no home runs and no attempted stolen bases
- Are hitting .228 against fastballs
- Are 2-for-16 with runners in scoring position, part of a 3-for-32 postseason disaster in those spots
This has been the year in which baseball made a sharp turn when it comes to the speed of the game. Younger players thrive. Velocity, and the widespread adoption of the family of three fastballs, changed everything. You need fast-twitch athleticism, youthfulness. You need this generation of players who know velocity as a first language. You need rangy players on defense. The numbers bear out that younger players are the preferred way to go.
Players 30 and younger this year hit .247. Players in the 31-35 year-old demographic hit 10 points worse, .237, their worst showing ever. There was a time when front offices valued those 31-35 players because it seemed to be the peak intersection of experience and physical tools. Front offices were afraid to commit to younger players because of the lack of reps and track records. Those days are over.
The difference on the field in NLCS Game 3 was striking. The Brewers are the fastest team in baseball, as measured by sprint speed. The Dodgers are 24th.
The Brewers started a lineup and a pitcher with an average age of 26.1. They became the first team in history with a second postseason game starting three players 22 and younger: leftfielder Jackson Chourio, shortstop Cooper Pratt and rightfielder Luis Lara. Chourio opened the game with a first-pitch homer. Pratt smacked three hits, stole a base and scored a run. Lara flew around rightfield like a bird of prey, snaring anything that dared enter his airspace.
Watching Chourio, 22, Garrett Mitchell, 28, and Lara, 21, patrol the outfield was like watching an Olympic sprint relay team.
On the other side of the field, the Dodgers, especially their bats, looked old and slow. The average age of their starting 10 was 32.3 years old—more than six years older than Milwaukee’s fearless group. Only two starting Dodgers were in their 20s: centerfielder Andy Pages, 25, and Kyle Tucker, 29, who with his diminished range and baserunning has been trending older than his age.
By starting eight players 31 and older, these Dodgers joined the 2023 Dodgers, who got bounced by the Diamondbacks, as the only teams in the past 19 postseasons to trot out so many starting players that old in a game.
Fittingly, the old team played an outdated style of baseball, one from a generation ago. The ninth-place hitter, Tommy Edman, twice batted after the leadoff runner reached first base. Twice manager Dave Roberts did not ask him to bunt.
“I thought about it, but it’s just, he had a good pitch to hit. Flew out,” Roberts said. “I just didn’t feel giving up an out right there. Early in the game, I wanted Tommy to hit ...
“We haven’t been getting hits with runners in scoring position. To give up an out, to bank on getting a hit with runners in scoring position, I’d rather just try to maybe slug, hit a double.”
Edman was a below average hitter (97 OPS+) with a .385 slug this season.
Roberts and the Dodgers keep waiting for slug to show up at the expense of forfeiting the situational baseball as deployed by the other three remaining teams, the youthful Brewers, Guardians and Rays. The Dodgers still may be waiting Thanksgiving morning.
For instance, the Dodgers were down 1-0 in the sixth when Roberts sent 36-year-old Max Muncy to hit for Pages with runners on first and second and no outs. In that situation, the Brewers are bunting. Milwaukee plays get-em-over, get-em-in ball. The Dodgers? No way. Muncy is a three-true outcome guy. He is not going to bunt. Again, the Dodgers played for slug and got nothing. Muncy struck out. Will Smith, 31, did save the rally with a two-run double. But the Dodgers would go 1-for-12 after that against hard-throwing relievers D.L. Hall and Trevor Megill.
The lineup remained cold. Shohei Ohtani, 32, cannot pull a baseball because of lower-half injuries that won’t allow him to properly turn his hips and get to a firm front side. Freeman, 37, has three extra-base hits since Aug. 31.
“[Our] pitching staff has been great, to be honest,” Rojas said. “It’s really hard to put it into context when you have to pitch and have to play defense with a one run lead every single time. It’s like asking these guys to just throw a perfect inning every single time. It’s not sustainable. So, the blame is on the offense. We all know we could’ve done better, but nothing we can do now.”
How in the world has Milwaukee made Los Angeles look so bad?
“It’s pretty simple,” Muncy said. “We’ve played like [poop]. They’ve played great.”
Occam’s razor (or commode) aside, the one-sided NLCS is bigger than that. It stands as a changing of the guard, recalling the 1964 World Series, when the St. Louis Cardinals, emblematic of the National League embracing Black and Latin American players, ended the dynasty of an aging New York Yankees team, then the second oldest team in baseball. The younger, faster, harder-throwing, more creative team has been, beyond doubt, the better team.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers set their lineup for their NLCS Game 4 matchup against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers set their lineup for their NLCS Game 4 matchup against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday.
The Dodgers currently face a 3-0 deficit in the series, and need to win Thursday’s game to keep their World Series hopes alive. They managed just two runs in Game 3 of the NLCS, the first of three potential games in Los Angeles.
Who is Pitching For the Dodgers?
As they announced before the start of the series, the Dodgers have Tyler Glasnow on the mound for the fourth game of the NLCS. Injuries cut Glasnow’s regular season short, allowing him to make just 22 starts while posting a 3.49 ERA, but he earned an all-important win for the team in Game 4 of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves.
He threw 4.2 innings while allowing just one earned run, though he allowed five walks in the process. The veteran right-hander will look to keep the Brewers off of the board to give the Dodgers some kind of advantage in Thursday’s game.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers made just one substitution in their lineup from Game 3, but drastically changed the order in which their hitters appear. Shohei Ohtani returned to the top of the lineup as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, followed by shortstop Mookie Betts and first baseman Freddie Freeman. Catcher Will Smith, after his two-run double in Wednesday’s loss, returns to the cleanup spot for the Dodgers, and right fielder Kyle Tucker follows him to the plate.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez will bat sixth, and Miguel Rojas remains in the lineup, though as the second baseman for Game 4. Batting eighth is center fielder Andy Pages, and Kiké Hernandez steps in at third base to round out the lineup.
Dodgers’ Lineup vs. Braves
1. Shohei Ohtani, DH
2. Mookie Betts, SS
3. Freddie Freeman, 1B
4. Will Smith, C
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
7. Miguel Rojas, 2B
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Kiké Hernandez, 3B
P. Tyler Glasnow, RHP.
When Does Thursday’s Game Start?
First pitch for Thursday’s game comes at 5:00 p.m. PT, moved up one hour from the original start time of 6:00 p.m. PT due to scheduling changes in the ALDS. The Dodgers will look to generate some offense and extend their season with a strong performance in Game 4.
